title: Magnetic metals: why a magnet attracts one coin and not another

summary.text: A magnet lifts a one-rupee coin and a two-rupee coin. It leaves a golden five-rupee coin and a ten-rupee coin on the table. All four are metal, so why does the magnet attract only two? Each coin is an alloy, which is a mixture of metals, and each alloy answers a magnet in its own way. Your child tests every coin in the house, and checks whether colour, shine or a name can tell them which metals are magnetic. They find that a one-rupee coin and a steel plate are both mostly iron, yet the magnet attracts only the coin. The reason is the way the iron atoms are packed. Being magnetic is something many atoms do together.
summary.art: A child's hand holding a magnet with a one-rupee coin and a two-rupee coin hanging from it, above a golden five-rupee coin and a ten-rupee coin lying on a table.

intro.hook: Put a one-rupee coin and a golden five-rupee coin on the table. Now think about a magnet. Which coin will the magnet lift: both, one, or neither? Say what you think, and why.
intro.text: Many people expect a magnet to attract every metal. Others expect it to attract every coin, or none. In the first activity, Four Coins and a Magnet, you test four coins and see. Then you test every coin in the house. In this unit you find out which metals are magnetic, and how to test them fairly. You also find out why two things made mostly of iron can give a magnet two different answers.
intro.art: A one-rupee coin and a golden five-rupee coin side by side on a wooden table, with a small magnet held just above them and a question mark between.

outcomes: By the end I can say how a magnet differs from a magnetic material, and find the magnet with the T test.
By the end I can name the magnetic metals, and say that most metals are not magnetic.
By the end I can say what an alloy is, and name the alloys in Indian coins and kitchen steel.
By the end I can plan a fair test of metals, with a prediction, a table and a conclusion.
By the end I can use my results to test a rule, and find the thing that breaks it.
By the end I can explain with atoms why a magnet attracts coin steel and not kitchen steel.
By the end I can say what a yes and a no from a magnet test really tell me.
By the end I can say what scientists still do not know about magnetic materials.

terms.meaning: A magnet is a thing with a magnetic field of its own. It can attract magnetic materials, and attract or repel other magnets.
terms.example: A fridge magnet holds a paper to the steel door by itself.
terms.art: A round magnet with faint curved field lines around it, holding a steel pin.

terms.meaning: A magnetic field is the space around a magnet where its force acts. We cannot see it.
terms.example: A coin jumps to a magnet before they touch, because the coin is already inside the field.
terms.art: A bar magnet with curved lines running from one end to the other, and a pin inside the lines.

terms.meaning: A magnetic material is a material that a magnet attracts. It has no magnetic field of its own.
terms.example: A steel nail is a magnetic material. Two nails do not attract each other.
terms.art: Two steel nails lying side by side, not moving, and a third nail hanging from a magnet.

terms.meaning: We call a material non-magnetic when an ordinary magnet does not attract it.
terms.example: Copper, aluminium, brass, gold and wood are non-magnetic.
terms.art: A magnet held above a brass key, a copper wire and a piece of foil, none of them moving.

terms.meaning: To attract is to pull something closer with a force.
terms.example: A magnet attracts a one-rupee coin.
terms.art: A coin sliding towards a magnet, with an arrow pointing at the magnet.

terms.meaning: A metal is a material that is usually shiny, carries heat and electricity well, and can be beaten into shape.
terms.example: Iron, copper, aluminium, gold and nickel are metals.
terms.art: A row of small samples: an iron nail, a copper wire, aluminium foil and a gold ring.

terms.meaning: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, melted together. Most of the other elements are metals too.
terms.example: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Steel is an alloy of iron and a little carbon.
terms.art: Two streams of melted metal, one reddish and one grey, pouring into one pot of yellow brass.

terms.meaning: Steel is an alloy made mostly of iron, with a little carbon. The carbon makes it harder than plain iron.
terms.example: Nails, safety pins and paper clips are made of steel.
terms.art: A steel nail, a safety pin and a paper clip on a table.

terms.meaning: Stainless steel is steel with chromium added, so that it does not rust. Some kinds also hold nickel or manganese.
terms.example: A steel plate and a one-rupee coin are two different kinds of stainless steel.
terms.art: A shiny steel plate beside a one-rupee coin.

terms.meaning: Brass is a yellow alloy of copper and zinc. A magnet does not attract it.
terms.example: Many lamps, bells and keys are made of brass.
terms.art: A brass oil lamp with a magnet held near it, the magnet not sticking.

terms.meaning: Cupronickel is a silver-coloured alloy of copper and nickel. The centre of a ten-rupee coin is cupronickel.
terms.example: The centre of a ten-rupee coin is three parts copper and one part nickel.
terms.art: A ten-rupee coin with its silver centre circled and labelled copper and nickel.

terms.meaning: An atom is one of the tiny particles that everything is made of. It is far too small to see.
terms.example: A one-rupee coin holds billions of billions of iron atoms.
terms.art: A coin with a zoom circle showing rows of tiny balls.

terms.meaning: A material is ferromagnetic when the tiny magnets of its atoms line up with their neighbours. A magnet attracts it strongly.
terms.example: Iron, nickel and cobalt are ferromagnetic at room temperature.
terms.art: A zoom circle of atoms, each with a small arrow, all the arrows pointing the same way.

terms.meaning: A property is something you can find out about a material by looking or testing.
terms.example: Colour, hardness and being magnetic are three properties of a metal.
terms.art: A spoon with three labels: silver colour, hard, and a magnet with a question mark.

terms.meaning: In a fair test you change one thing and keep everything else the same.
terms.example: To compare coins fairly, use the same magnet, held the same way, on every coin.
terms.art: A child lowering the same magnet onto a row of different coins, one at a time.

terms.meaning: A prediction is a guess made before a test, with a reason for it.
terms.example: I predict the magnet will lift the nail, because nails are steel.
terms.art: A notebook page with the word 'I predict' and a drawing of a magnet and a nail.

terms.meaning: A conclusion is what your results let you say at the end of a test.
terms.example: My conclusion is that colour does not tell me which coins are magnetic.
terms.art: A results table with a ringed sentence written underneath.

explanations.concept: A magnet and a magnetic material are different things
explanations.definition: A magnet has a magnetic field of its own. A magnetic material is attracted by a magnet, but has no field of its own.
explanations.description: A magnet attracts a steel nail, and it can attract or repel another magnet. A steel nail is only a magnetic material. Put two nails together and nothing happens, because neither has a field of its own. While a nail touches a magnet, the nail acts as a magnet for a short time and can lift a pin. Take the magnet away and the nail soon stops. So there are three kinds of thing: magnets, magnetic materials and non-magnetic materials. There is a test that needs only the two bars themselves. Touch the end of one bar to the middle of the other, like the letter T. A bar magnet is strong at its ends and weak in its middle. So the bar whose end holds on to the other's middle is the magnet.
examples: In Two Nails, Then the T Test, two nails lay side by side and did not attract each other.
A fridge door is a magnetic material. It attracts no pins, but a magnet sticks to it.
Two fridge magnets can push each other apart. A magnet and a nail never push apart.
explanations.art: Three small drawings: two nails doing nothing, a magnet holding a nail, and one bar touching the middle of another bar in a T shape.

explanations.concept: Only a few metals are magnetic
explanations.definition: At room temperature, only three pure metals are strongly magnetic: iron, nickel and cobalt.
explanations.description: There are about ninety metals among the elements. A magnet strongly attracts only iron, nickel and cobalt. A fourth metal, gadolinium, joins them only when it is cooler than about 20 degrees Celsius. All the other pure metals, such as copper, aluminium, zinc, tin, lead, silver and gold, are not attracted by an ordinary magnet. So being magnetic is rare among metals. It only seems common because iron is common. About a third of the Earth's mass is iron, and steel is the most used metal of all.
examples: A magnet attracts an iron tawa and a steel nail. It does not attract copper wire or aluminium foil.
Gold and silver jewellery is not attracted. A steel spring inside a clasp is.
Gadolinium is magnetic on a cool morning and not on a hot afternoon.
explanations.art: A long row of ninety small metal squares, with only three of them, labelled iron, nickel and cobalt, drawn clinging to a magnet.

explanations.concept: An alloy is a mixture of metals
explanations.definition: An alloy is a metal melted and mixed with one or more other elements. When it cools, the atoms of the different elements are mixed together in one solid.
explanations.description: Very few metal things at home are one pure metal. Steel is iron with a little carbon. Stainless steel is steel with chromium, which stops rust. Brass is copper with zinc, and bronze is copper with tin. People make alloys because an alloy can be harder, cheaper or longer lasting than a pure metal. Pure iron is quite soft and rusts fast, and steel is hard. Pure gold bends too easily for a bangle, so jewellers mix in a little copper and silver. When you test a thing made of an alloy, you test all its metals together.
examples: A brass lamp from Nachiarkoil in Tamil Nadu is copper and zinc.
Gold stamped 916 is 91.6 parts gold in every 100. The rest is mostly copper and silver.
The golden five-rupee coin is nickel-brass: copper, zinc and a little nickel.
explanations.art: A zoom circle into a piece of brass showing two kinds of tiny balls, orange and grey, mixed together in neat rows.

explanations.concept: Indian coins are made of four different alloys
explanations.definition: The coins in use today are made of stainless steel, nickel-brass, aluminium-bronze and cupronickel. A magnet attracts only the stainless steel.
explanations.description: One-rupee coins have been made of a stainless steel since 1992. Two-rupee coins have been made of the same steel since about 2007. This coin steel is iron with about one sixth chromium, and a magnet attracts it. The golden five-rupee coin, made in recent years, is nickel-brass. A ten-rupee coin has two alloys. Its golden ring is aluminium-bronze, which is copper with a little aluminium. Its silver centre is cupronickel. A magnet attracts neither part. Older coins can differ. Old two-rupee coins with eleven sides are cupronickel. Thick old five-rupee coins are cupronickel too. For a short time in the late 2000s, some five-rupee coins are said to have been made of steel. Mints change the alloy when a metal becomes too costly. Steel costs less than copper and nickel.
examples: In the Coin Year Test, the magnet lifted the one-rupee and two-rupee coins.
The magnet left the golden five-rupee coin and the ten-rupee coin on the table.
An eleven-sided two-rupee coin from the 1990s is not attracted, though it is worth the same.
explanations.art: Four Indian coins in a row, each with a label under it naming its alloy, and a magnet above the first two.

explanations.concept: The list of metals in an alloy does not tell you whether it is magnetic
explanations.definition: An alloy can be non-magnetic though it holds a magnetic metal. An alloy can be magnetic though none of its metals is.
explanations.description: Nickel is a magnetic metal. The centre of a ten-rupee coin is one quarter nickel, and a magnet does not attract it. A steel plate is about seven tenths iron, and a magnet does not attract it either. Railway crossings are made of a steel with about 13 parts manganese in every 100. It is mostly iron, and a magnet hardly attracts it. The wire that glows in an electric heater is four fifths nickel, and it is not magnetic. The surprise also runs the other way. In 1903 Friedrich Heusler mixed copper, manganese and aluminium. None of the three is magnetic, yet a magnet attracted the alloy strongly. So you cannot add up the metals in the recipe. You have to test the alloy itself.
examples: The centre of a ten-rupee coin is cupronickel. It is about one quarter nickel, yet a magnet does not attract it.
Kitchen stainless steel is mostly iron. Even so, a magnet does not attract it, or attracts it only faintly.
Heusler's alloy is made only of copper, manganese and aluminium. None of them is magnetic, and a magnet still attracts the alloy strongly.
explanations.art: Two recipe cards side by side: one says copper plus nickel with a crossed-out magnet, the other says copper plus manganese plus aluminium with a magnet holding the metal.

explanations.concept: Every iron atom is a tiny magnet
explanations.definition: Each iron atom has a very small magnetic field of its own, which comes from its electrons. So does each nickel atom and each cobalt atom.
explanations.description: An electron is one of the tiny particles in every atom, and every electron is a tiny magnet. In most atoms the electrons are in pairs that point opposite ways and cancel. In an atom of iron, nickel or cobalt, a few electrons are left unpaired, so the whole atom is a tiny magnet. One atom's field is far too weak to notice. A magnet attracts a nail strongly only because the tiny magnets of billions of iron atoms point the same way and their fields add up. If neighbouring atoms point in different ways, their fields cancel, and the magnet finds almost nothing to hold.
examples: A one-rupee coin holds more than ten thousand billion billion iron atoms.
In a steel nail, groups of atoms called domains each point one way. A magnet nearby turns them to face it.
Your blood holds iron, but the iron atoms are spread far apart. Because they are not packed together in a crowd, a magnet does not attract blood.
explanations.art: A zoom circle into a nail showing rows of tiny balls, each with a small arrow, all pointing the same way.

explanations.concept: Why a magnet attracts coin steel and not kitchen steel
explanations.description: A one-rupee coin and a steel plate are both mostly iron, with chromium to stop rust. The plate also holds nickel or manganese. These extra metals make the iron atoms pack in a different pattern. In coin steel, each iron atom has 8 nearest neighbours, as in plain iron. Scientists call this steel ferritic. In kitchen steel, each atom has 12 nearest neighbours, packed more tightly. Scientists call this steel austenitic. In the first pattern, the tiny magnets of neighbouring atoms line up with each other. In the second pattern, they do not line up, so their fields cancel. This account is simplified. The full reason why one packing lines up and the other does not needs quantum physics, and it is still hard to calculate. What X-ray pictures show for certain is that the two steels are packed differently.
examples: In Same Coins, Two Patterns, the same coins touched 4 neighbours in one pattern and 6 in the other.
Bend or press a kitchen steel vessel hard, and some of it changes to the other packing. That is why a magnet may cling faintly near a rim.
Above 912 degrees Celsius, even pure iron changes to the tighter packing.
explanations.art: Two zoom circles: on the left a cube of balls with one ball in the middle and arrows all pointing the same way, on the right a tighter stack of balls with arrows pointing different ways.

explanations.concept: Being magnetic is something many atoms do together
explanations.definition: A material is ferromagnetic when the tiny magnets of neighbouring atoms line up with each other by themselves. This lining up belongs to the whole group of atoms.
explanations.description: We say 'iron is magnetic', as if each iron atom carried the property inside. But the same iron atoms give three different answers. In a nail they line up, and a magnet attracts the nail strongly. In a steel plate they are packed differently, and the magnet does not attract the plate. In iron hotter than 770 degrees Celsius the atoms shake too hard to stay lined up, and the magnet lets go. In all three, each atom is still a tiny magnet. What changes is whether the neighbours line up. So 'magnetic' describes what a great many atoms do together.
examples: Pierre Curie showed in 1895 that iron stops being attracted above a fixed temperature, and is attracted again when it cools.
Kitchen steel and coin steel hold the same kind of iron atoms, in different packings.
The nickel atoms in cupronickel sit among copper atoms, and their tiny magnets do not line up.
explanations.art: Three zoom circles of the same balls with arrows: lined up in a nail, pointing different ways in a steel plate, and shaking in all directions in red-hot iron.

explanations.concept: No clue you can see tells you whether a metal is magnetic
explanations.definition: Colour, shine and the name 'steel' do not tell you whether a magnet will attract a metal thing. Only a test with a magnet does.
explanations.description: Many people use a quick rule, such as 'silver-coloured metals are magnetic'. A rule like this can be tested. Look for one thing that breaks it. Aluminium foil is silver-coloured, and a magnet does not attract it. That one thing is enough to show the rule is wrong. 'Shiny metals are magnetic' is broken by a brass lamp. 'Dull metals are not magnetic' is broken by a black iron tawa. 'Everything called steel is magnetic' is broken by a steel plate. A rule that fits ten things can still be wrong. One thing that breaks it settles the matter. Fitting more things only makes a rule more likely to be right.
examples: In Can You Tell by Looking?, a one-rupee coin and a steel plate looked alike and gave different answers.
A black tawa and a shiny safety pin look different and both are attracted.
The cap of a glass soda bottle looks painted, but it is thin steel, and a magnet lifts it.
explanations.art: A magnet between two look-alike silver things, a coin clinging to it and a steel plate not, with a brass lamp and a black tawa in the background.

explanations.definition: A fair test of metals uses the same magnet, held the same way, on one thing at a time, with a prediction first and every result written down.
explanations.description: The thing you change is the metal thing being tested. The thing you watch is whether the magnet lifts or holds it. Everything else stays the same: the magnet, the face of the magnet you use, and how you bring it near. Write your prediction before each test, so that you cannot change it afterwards. Write 'yes', 'no' or 'weak' for every thing, even the dull ones. A strong magnet gives more 'weak' answers than a weak magnet, so say which magnet you used. Test more than one spot on a big thing, because a handle, a rivet or a base may be a different metal.
examples: In the Coin Year Test, every coin lay flat on the table and met the same face of the same magnet.
A pressure cooker can be aluminium with a steel plate in its base, so its side and its base answer differently.
A result of 'weak' on a steel tumbler is still a result. Write it down.
explanations.art: A notebook table with columns for the thing, the prediction and the result, beside a magnet and a row of small metal things.

explanations.concept: What a magnet test can and cannot tell you
explanations.definition: A 'yes' shows that something magnetic is within reach of the magnet. A 'no' shows that nothing magnetic enough is within reach. Neither tells you the whole recipe.
explanations.description: A magnet test answers one small question about one spot. It can be fooled in two ways. A thing can say yes because magnetic metal is hidden inside it, like a steel coin wrapped in foil, or steel under a thin coat of brass. A thing can say no because its magnetic part is too far inside, or because its alloy is one the magnet does not attract. So a yes on a 'gold' chain shows it has steel in it. A no does not show the chain is gold, because brass says no too. A magnet test is quick and useful. It is strongest when it is used with other tests, such as colour, mass and the stamp on the metal.
examples: In Fool the Magnet Test, a ball of foil with a coin inside clung to the magnet.
A magnet sticks to a 'brass' sheet that is really steel with a thin brass coat.
A magnet does not stick to a steel plate, and the plate is still mostly iron.
explanations.art: A magnet lifting a ball of foil, with a cut-away view showing a coin hidden inside the ball.

explanations.concept: Choosing an alloy for the job: bone pins and scanners
explanations.definition: Engineers choose an alloy partly by how it answers a magnet. Some jobs need a magnetic alloy, and some need one that a magnet does not attract.
explanations.description: A hospital MRI scanner takes pictures of the inside of a body with a very strong magnet. A common hospital scanner has a field about 30,000 times as strong as the Earth's magnetic field, and some are stronger. A loose iron thing near it would fly towards it. So the pins and plates that surgeons put in a broken bone are made of titanium alloy, or of a stainless steel that a magnet does not attract. A compass case is made of brass, so that it does not disturb the needle. Other jobs need the opposite. The base of a pan for an induction stove must be a magnetic steel. The core of a motor is a soft magnetic steel with a little silicon in it.
examples: Before an MRI scan, people are asked to take off keys, hairpins and belts.
A ship built to find sea mines has a hull that magnets do not attract.
A fridge door seal holds because the fridge door is a magnetic steel.
explanations.art: A hospital scanner shaped like a large ring, with a small drawing beside it of a mended arm bone held by a metal plate.

explanations.concept: The same carbon atoms give two answers to a magnet
explanations.definition: Graphite and diamond are both made only of carbon atoms. A strong magnet pushes graphite away far more than it pushes diamond.
explanations.description: A very strong magnet pushes weakly on materials we call non-magnetic. The push on graphite, the grey material in pencil lead, is one of the largest. In graphite the carbon atoms lie in flat sheets, and electrons can move around rings of atoms in each sheet. In diamond the same atoms are joined in a different pattern, and the push is much smaller. In the 1930s Kathleen Lonsdale and K. S. Krishnan measured how crystals answer a magnet in different directions. Their numbers showed that the pattern of the atoms sets the answer. The same thing is true of the two steels. Coin steel and kitchen steel hold the same iron atoms, and only the pattern is different.
examples: A thin pencil lead can be pushed aside by a very strong magnet.
Lonsdale and Krishnan published their measurements together in 1936.
Coin steel and kitchen steel show the same idea with iron. The atoms are the same, and the pattern decides how a magnet answers.
explanations.art: Two zoom circles, one showing carbon atoms in flat honeycomb sheets labelled graphite and one showing a tight three-dimensional net labelled diamond.

explanations.concept: Iron and nickel from space, and a magnet nobody could make
explanations.description: Iron meteorites are pieces of metal that fall from space. They are an alloy of iron and nickel, from the middle of small worlds that broke apart long ago. A magnet attracts them. In some meteorites that cooled over millions of years, the iron and nickel atoms sorted themselves into neat layers, one layer of each. This layered alloy is called tetrataenite. It is a strong permanent magnet, though it holds only iron and nickel. For a long time nobody could make it, because the atoms sort themselves far too slowly. In 2022 a team in Cambridge reported that adding phosphorus lets the layers form in seconds. Other scientists are still checking how well this works. If it does, strong magnets could be made from two common metals.
examples: The Earth's core is also an iron and nickel alloy, but it is too hot to be a permanent magnet.
Today's strongest magnets need neodymium, which is costly to mine and clean.
The same two metals, mixed without layers, make a much weaker magnet.
explanations.art: A dark iron meteorite cut open to show a criss-cross metal pattern, with a zoom circle of two kinds of balls stacked in alternate layers.

agreed.text: A magnet strongly attracts iron, nickel and cobalt, and many alloys that hold them. It does not attract most other metals.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can repeat the test at home, and laboratories measure the same thing with exact instruments.

agreed.text: A magnetic material has no magnetic field of its own. Two pieces of plain steel do not attract each other.
agreed.evidence: Two nails lie side by side without moving. Each one is attracted when a magnet is brought near.

agreed.text: The metals in an alloy do not tell you whether the alloy is magnetic.
agreed.evidence: Robert Hadfield's manganese steel of 1882 is mostly iron and hardly magnetic. Friedrich Heusler's alloy of 1903 has no magnetic metal in it and is strongly magnetic.

agreed.text: Strong magnetism comes from the tiny magnets of many atoms lining up with each other.
agreed.evidence: Iron stops being attracted above 770 degrees Celsius and is attracted again when it cools, as Pierre Curie measured in 1895. The atoms are the same throughout.

agreed.text: The way atoms are packed in a metal changes how the metal answers a magnet.
agreed.evidence: X-ray pictures show different packings in magnetic and non-magnetic stainless steels. Heusler's alloy is magnetic only when its atoms are in an ordered pattern.

agreed.text: Indian coins of the same value have been made of different alloys in different years.
agreed.evidence: The mints publish the metal of each coin. A magnet attracts a new two-rupee coin and not an old eleven-sided one.

challenging.claim: If a metal thing has iron in it, a magnet will attract it.
challenging.who: Many people, and some school books
challenging.for: It is true for nails, pins, tawas and most things made of plain steel.
challenging.against: A steel plate is about seven tenths iron and is not attracted. Railway crossing steel is mostly iron and is hardly attracted. What matters is how the iron atoms are packed.
challenging.context: This card is about a common rule: iron inside a thing always makes it magnetic.

challenging.claim: Steel vessels that a magnet sticks to are poor quality.
challenging.who: Some shopkeepers and shoppers in India
challenging.for: The best-known kitchen steel, called 304, is hardly attracted. So a strong pull shows that a vessel is some other steel.
challenging.against: A magnet tells you how the atoms are packed. It does not tell you how well a steel resists rust. Some cheaper steels are not attracted either. Some good steels, used for spoons and induction pans, are attracted.
challenging.context: This card is about a test that people use in steel vessel shops: touch a magnet to the vessel.

challenging.claim: A magnet can tell a real coin from a fake one.
challenging.who: Makers of ticket and vending machines
challenging.for: Machines do check how a coin answers a magnet and how it carries electricity. A fake made of the wrong alloy usually fails.
challenging.against: A magnet alone gives only yes or no. A fake made of any steel would pass as a one-rupee coin. Machines also measure size, mass and other properties.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a magnet test alone can catch a fake coin.

challenging.claim: A magnetic alloy must have iron, nickel or cobalt in it.
challenging.for: Every magnetic alloy known then held at least one of the three.
challenging.against: Heusler's alloy of copper, manganese and aluminium is strongly magnetic. Later alloys without the three metals have been made too.
challenging.context: This card is about an old belief: only iron, nickel or cobalt can make an alloy magnetic.

challenging.claim: Everything a metal does can be worked out from its atoms alone.
challenging.for: The laws that atoms and electrons follow are well known. Nothing in an alloy breaks those laws.
challenging.against: In 1972 the physicist Philip Anderson wrote that large groups of atoms behave in ways that cannot in practice be worked out from one atom. Even today, nobody can calculate exactly the temperature at which iron stops being magnetic.
challenging.context: This card is about a deep question: can the properties of a metal be worked out from its atoms alone?

challenging.claim: A magnet that does not stick proves that a chain is real gold.
challenging.for: Gold is not attracted, so a chain that sticks to a magnet has steel in it and is not solid gold.
challenging.against: Brass, copper and many other cheap alloys are not attracted either. The clasp of a real gold chain can stick, because it has a steel spring. A 'no' rules out steel and nothing more.
challenging.context: This card is about using a magnet to check gold jewellery.

big_questions.q: A coin and a steel plate hold the same iron atoms. So where is the 'magnetic': in the atoms, or in the way they are packed?
big_questions.hint: Think about what changed between the coin and the plate, and what stayed the same.

big_questions.q: One thing that breaks a rule is enough to end it. How many things that fit a rule are enough to prove it?
big_questions.hint: Before 1903, every magnetic alloy that anyone had tested held iron, nickel or cobalt.

big_questions.q: A coin from 1998 and a coin from 2015 are different metals and buy the same things. What makes a coin worth two rupees?
big_questions.hint: Think about what would happen if a shopkeeper refused the older coin.

big_questions.q: Your body is a crowd of cells. What can you do that no single cell of yours does?
big_questions.hint: A coin is attracted to a magnet strongly, and one iron atom hardly at all.

big_questions.q: People have long paid more for gold than for iron. Yet magnets, bridges and blood all need iron. Who decides which metal is precious?
big_questions.hint: Compare what each metal can do with how rare each one is.

big_questions.q: Scientists were sure in 1900 that a magnetic alloy needed iron, nickel or cobalt. How should we treat the things we are sure of today?
big_questions.hint: Being sure and being right are two different things. What would change your mind?

story.title: The Coin That Went the Wrong Way
story.note: A made-up story. The science is real. Indian two-rupee coins made in the 1990s have eleven sides and are cupronickel, which a magnet does not attract. Two-rupee coins made since about 2007 are a stainless steel that a magnet attracts. Visakhapatnam really has a large steel plant. Sravani, Lakshmamma, the judge, the school and the machine are imagined.
text: Every afternoon at half past one, Lakshmamma counted coins. She ran the canteen at the school in Visakhapatnam, and children paid for their idlis and lemon rice in coins. By the end of lunch the steel bowl beside her stove was full.

Sravani, who was ten, often stayed to help. She liked the sound the coins made. She did not like how long it took. There were ones in one heap, twos in another, and then fives and tens. Lakshmamma's fingers were quick, but the heap was always big.

Three weeks before Science Day, Sravani found a round black magnet in her uncle's box of broken things. It had come out of an old speaker. She took it to the canteen and dipped it into the bowl, just to see.
It came up bristling with coins. She looked at them. Every one was a one or a two. She dipped again. Ones and twos. Not a single golden five clung to it, and not a single ten.
'It likes the small money,' said Lakshmamma, and laughed.

That night Sravani drew a machine. It took her nine days and two shoe boxes to build it. A coin went in at the top and slid flat down a cardboard slope. Halfway down, under the cardboard, sat the speaker magnet. A one or a two stopped dead above the magnet, as if a hand had caught it. A five or a ten slid past and dropped into a cup at the bottom. A cardboard flap swept the caught coins sideways into a second cup.

She tested it with the whole canteen bowl, four hundred and twelve coins. It did not make one mistake. She painted a sign for the front: COIN SORTER. ONES AND TWOS TO THE LEFT. FIVES AND TENS TO THE RIGHT.

On Science Day the school hall was full of tables. There was a volcano, a water filter and three solar cookers. The judge was a tall man with a steel plant badge on his shirt. He stopped at each table and asked one question.
At Sravani's table he asked nothing. He read her sign, took a coin from his own pocket and dropped it in at the top.
It was a two-rupee coin. Sravani saw the big 2 on it as it went by. It slid down the slope, passed over the magnet without slowing at all, and fell into the cup for fives and tens.
Somebody behind the judge laughed. 'Your machine cannot count,' said a boy from Class 7.

Sravani's face went hot. Four hundred and twelve coins, and it had to go wrong now. She wanted to say that the slope was bumped, or that the coin was thrown too hard. But she had watched it. The coin had gone past the magnet as if the magnet were not there.

She picked the coin out of the cup and held it. It was a little heavier than the twos she knew. She turned it. It had corners. She counted them with her thumbnail: eleven sides. Under the lions was a year, 1998.

She took a canteen two from the other cup. It was round, and its year was 2014. She held the speaker magnet near it and the coin jumped on with a click. She held the magnet near the judge's coin. Nothing. She pressed them together and let go, and the old coin fell on the table and spun.

'The machine did not make a mistake,' she said slowly. She was working it out as she spoke. 'It cannot read the number. It never could. It asks each coin one question. Are you made of the metal a magnet attracts? This coin said no.'
'It is a two-rupee coin,' said the boy.
'It is worth two rupees,' said Sravani. 'It is not made of the same metal. Somebody changed the metal and kept the number.'

Lakshmamma had come over from the canteen with flour on her hands. 'Those old ones with the corners,' she said. 'I have not seen one in years. They always felt heavier in the palm. I thought the new ones were only thinner.'
'Does anybody have more old coins?' Sravani asked the crowd.

The watchman's mother, who sold guavas at the gate, untied a knot in the end of her sari. She had kept three coins there since her daughter's wedding. One was a thick five-rupee coin, silver-coloured and heavy. Two were twos with corners. Sravani sent all three down the slope. All three slid past the magnet and fell to the right.
The judge was smiling now. 'So what does your machine sort?' he asked. It was his one question.
Sravani looked at her sign. Then she turned it over and borrowed a marker. She wrote on the back in large letters: STEEL COINS TO THE LEFT. ALL OTHER COINS TO THE RIGHT. CHECK THE OLD ONES BY HAND.
'That is a more honest sign,' said the judge. 'In my work we test every batch of steel, even when the label says what it is. The label is what somebody wrote. The test is what the metal does.'

The next afternoon the machine stood beside the stove in the canteen. Lakshmamma poured in the bowl, a handful at a time, and the coins clicked left and right. Once in a while a coin with corners slid to the wrong side. Each time, she held it up to the light, read its year aloud and dropped it in a jar on the shelf.

By the end of the term there were seven coins in the jar. Sravani asked if she could keep them. She did not spend them. She taped them in a row in her science notebook, oldest first, and under each one she wrote its year and one more word: NO.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a magnet does not read the number on a coin. It responds only to the metal. Indian one-rupee and two-rupee coins made today are a stainless steel that a magnet attracts. Five-rupee and ten-rupee coins are copper alloys that a magnet does not attract. Older two-rupee coins with eleven sides are cupronickel, a copper and nickel alloy, so the magnet does not attract them, though they are worth the same. The machine sorted by material all along. The value stamped on a coin and the metal it is made of are two separate facts, and only a test finds the second.
ask: The machine sorted 412 coins without a mistake. Why did it send the judge's coin the other way?
What question does the magnet ask each coin?
Why did Sravani change her sign?
The old coin and the new coin are both worth two rupees. What is different about them?
The judge tests steel even when the label says what it is. Why?

games.title: Alloy Bets
games.context: This is a card game about alloys. Each card gives the recipe of one alloy. You bet beans on whether a magnet attracts it, then turn the card to check.

printables.title: 20 alloy cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Nail steel. Used for nails, pins and paper clips. Recipe: iron with a little carbon. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: Yes. It is nearly all iron, packed as in plain iron.

items.f: Cast iron. Used for a tawa or a kadai. Recipe: iron with 2 to 4 parts carbon in 100. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: Yes. The carbon makes it hard and brittle, and the iron atoms still line up.

items.f: Coin steel. Used for one-rupee and two-rupee coins. Recipe: iron with about one sixth chromium. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: Yes. The chromium stops rust and leaves the packing of plain iron.

items.f: Kitchen stainless steel. Used for plates, tumblers and tiffin boxes. Recipe: iron, chromium and nickel or manganese. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: No, or only faintly. The extra metals change the packing of the iron atoms.

items.f: Brass. Used for lamps, bells and keys. Recipe: copper and zinc. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: No. Neither copper nor zinc is magnetic, and nor is their alloy.

items.f: Bronze. Used for temple bells and statues. Recipe: copper and tin. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: No. Neither metal is magnetic, and nor is their alloy.

items.f: Cupronickel. Used for the centre of a ten-rupee coin. Recipe: three parts copper and one part nickel. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: No. The nickel atoms sit among copper atoms and do not line up.

items.f: Nickel-brass. Used for the golden five-rupee coin. Recipe: copper, zinc and a little nickel. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: No. It holds far too little nickel, spread among the other atoms.

items.f: Aluminium-bronze. Used for the golden ring of a ten-rupee coin. Recipe: copper with a little aluminium. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: No. Neither metal is magnetic, and nor is their alloy.

items.f: 22-carat gold. Used for bangles and chains. Recipe: 91.6 parts gold in 100, with copper and silver. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: No. None of the three is magnetic. A clasp may stick, because of a steel spring.

items.f: German silver. Used for trays, zips and some musical instruments. Recipe: copper, zinc and nickel, with no silver at all. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: No. The nickel is spread among copper and zinc atoms.

items.f: Solder. Used to join wires in a radio or a phone. Recipe: mostly tin, with a little copper or lead. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: No. None of these metals is magnetic.

items.f: Duralumin. Used for the bodies of aeroplanes. Recipe: aluminium with a little copper. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: No. Neither metal is magnetic. It is chosen because it is light and strong.

items.f: Alnico. Used in old loudspeakers and guitar pickups. Recipe: iron with aluminium, nickel and cobalt. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: Yes, strongly. It is one of the alloys that permanent magnets are made from.

items.f: Manganese steel. Used for railway crossings and rock crushers. Recipe: iron with about 13 parts manganese in 100. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: Hardly at all. It is mostly iron, but the manganese changes the packing of the atoms.

items.f: Heusler's alloy. Made first in 1903, and studied in laboratories. Recipe: copper, manganese and aluminium. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: Yes, strongly. None of its metals is magnetic. In this ordered pattern the manganese atoms line up.

items.f: Nichrome. Used for the glowing wire in a heater or a toaster. Recipe: four parts nickel and one part chromium. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: No. It is mostly nickel, yet the chromium stops the nickel atoms lining up.

items.f: Permalloy. Used to shield instruments from magnetic fields. Recipe: four parts nickel and one part iron. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: Yes, very easily. Both metals are magnetic, and this mix lines up at the lightest touch of a field.

items.f: Neodymium magnet alloy. Used in earphones, motors and hard disks. Recipe: neodymium, iron and boron. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: Yes, strongly. It makes the strongest permanent magnets in common use.

items.f: Invar. Used in precise clocks and measuring tapes. Recipe: about two parts iron and one part nickel. Will a magnet attract it?
items.b: Yes. Both metals are magnetic. It is chosen because it hardly grows when warmed.

printables.title: 2 bet mats for each player to copy: YES and NO
items: NO: a magnet does not attract it

rules: Each player takes 10 dry beans and copies the two bet mats on paper. Put 40 more beans in a bowl as the bank.
One player reads the top card aloud: the alloy, its use and its recipe.
Every player hides a hand over their mats and puts 1 or 2 beans on YES or on NO.
Turn the card over. If the answer is 'hardly at all' or 'only faintly', NO is right.
A right bet wins the same number of beans from the bank. A wrong bet goes to the bank.
A player with no beans takes 2 from the bank and plays on.
After 20 cards, the player with the most beans wins.
Playing alone: start with 10 beans. Try to finish with more than 20, then play again.

flow.kid: Read the card. Bet 1 or 2 beans on YES or NO. Turn the card. Read the reason.

A magnet will surely not attract it
You must test it to know

games.title: Fish for Change
games.context: This is a fishing game with real coins. You dip a magnet on a thread into a bowl of mixed coins. You try to catch exactly the amount on a target card.
rules: Put at least 8 one-rupee coins, 6 two-rupee coins, 3 five-rupee coins and 2 ten-rupee coins in a bowl. Cover the bowl with a cloth.
Tie a magnet to a thread 40 centimetres long. Tie the other end to a pencil. This is the rod.
On your turn, take the top target card. Lower the magnet under the cloth and lift it out.
Add up the coins on the magnet. You may dip again to catch more, as often as you like.
If your total is exactly the target, keep the card. If it goes over, you are bust: the card goes to the bottom of the pile.
Before any dip you may shake the rod once. Coins that fall go back in the bowl.
After your turn, put your coins back and pass the rod. The first player to keep 3 cards wins.
Playing alone: count how many turns you need to keep 3 cards. Then try to beat that number.

setup.art: A round magnet tied to a thread that hangs from a pencil, beside a bowl of mixed Indian coins.
setup.caption: 1. Tie a magnet to a thread and a pencil. Put mixed coins in a bowl.

setup.art: A child lowering the magnet on its thread under a cloth that covers the bowl, with a target card on the table.
setup.caption: 2. Take a target card. Dip the magnet under the cloth.

setup.art: The magnet lifted out with three silver-coloured coins clinging to it, and the child adding them up on fingers.
setup.caption: 3. Add up your catch. Hit the target exactly to keep the card.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 10 target cards and shuffle them. 2. Put the coins in a bowl and cover it with a cloth. 3. Tie the magnet to the thread and the pencil. 4. Ask which coins your child expects to catch, and why.
flow.say: We are going fishing for coins. Which coins do you think this rod will catch? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Shuffle the target cards. Cover the bowl of coins. Tie the magnet to the thread. Which coins will it catch?
flow.parent: Use the strongest small magnet you have. A thin bendy fridge magnet lifts one coin at most. A round black magnet from a magnet set lifts several.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fish for Change. Here you make the rod and set up the bowl.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. 2. Each player takes a target card and dips. 3. Count the catch aloud. 4. Dip again, shake once, or stop.
flow.say: Count your catch aloud. You have 5 rupees and need 7. Will you dip again or shake some off?
flow.kid: Take a card. Dip the magnet. Add up your coins. Dip again or stop.

ask.q: You need 5 rupees. Can you catch a five-rupee coin with this rod?
good: No. The magnet does not attract the golden five-rupee coin.
I have to make 5 from ones and twos.

flow.context: This is the main part of Fish for Change. Here you dip for coins and add them up.

flow.do: 1. Stop when a player has 3 cards. 2. Tip out the bowl. 3. Ask which coins never came up, and why.
flow.say: Look at the coins left in the bowl. Which kinds did nobody catch in the whole game? Why?
flow.kid: Tip out the bowl. Which coins did nobody catch? Say why.

check.q: In Fish for Change, the magnet never lifted a ten-rupee coin. Why?
options: A ten-rupee coin is too heavy
Its two alloys are not magnetic
It lay at the bottom of the bowl
check.why: The ring is aluminium-bronze and the centre is cupronickel. A magnet attracts neither. Choosing 'too heavy' forgets that the magnet gives no pull at all on that coin, even when they touch.

flow.context: This is the last step of Fish for Change. Here you look at the coins that the magnet never caught.

experiments.title: The Coin Year Test: which coins does a magnet attract?
experiments.context: In this experiment you test every coin in the house with a magnet. You write down each coin's value, colour and year. Then you find out which of the three tells you whether a magnet attracts the coin.
experiments.question: Which coins does a magnet attract? Does the value, the colour or the year of a coin tell you the answer before you test it?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which will tell you whether a magnet attracts a coin: its value, its colour, its year, or none of them? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the coin. Use the same magnet and the same face of the magnet every time. Lay each coin flat on the table. Lower the magnet until it touches the coin, then lift it 5 centimetres. Write 'yes' only if the coin comes up with the magnet. Test every coin, even when you feel sure of the answer.

materials.item: coins of every value you can find, at least 20 in all
a magnet that can lift a steel spoon by its handle, or 3 paper clips in a chain
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera, to read small years
a notebook, a pencil and a ruler

experiments.safety: Keep coins and small magnets away from children under three, who may swallow them. Wash your hands after handling coins.

schedule.what: Collect and sort the coins. Guess, test each coin, and look for a pattern by value, by colour and by year.

experiments.record: Fill in one row of the table for every coin. Then write three counts: how many coins of each value the magnet lifted, how many of each colour, and the oldest and newest year for 'yes' and for 'no'. Last, write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

flow.do: 1. Collect coins from purses, a piggy bank and drawers. 2. Sort them into rows by value. 3. Draw the table with four columns. 4. Write the value, the year and the colour of each coin.
flow.say: Let's find every coin in the house. Each coin has a year near its edge. Write the value, the year and the colour.
flow.kid: Collect all the coins. Sort them by value. Write each coin's value, year and colour.
flow.parent: The year is small. Use a magnifying glass, or take a phone photo and zoom in. For colour, write 'silver', 'golden' or 'both'. Ask an older relative or a neighbour for old coins, if you can.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Coin Year Test. Here you collect the coins and write down what you can see.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child which clue will give the answer: value, colour, year or none. 2. Ask for the reason. 3. Write both down.
flow.say: Before we test, which of these will tell us the answer: the value, the colour or the year? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which clue will work: value, colour, year or none. Say why. Write it down.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Silver coins look like steel, so colour will work.
Coins of one value are all the same, so value will work.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. In Four Coins and a Magnet your child saw only four coins. Many children now expect value to work every time.
flow.context: This step of the Coin Year Test is for guessing. You guess before you test the coins.

flow.do: 1. Lay the first coin flat on the table. 2. Lower the magnet until it touches the coin. 3. Lift the magnet 5 centimetres. 4. Write 'yes' or 'no'. 5. Do the same for every coin.
flow.say: Use the same face of the magnet each time. Lift it as high as this mark on the ruler. Write the answer at once.
flow.kid: Lay a coin flat. Touch it with the magnet. Lift the magnet 5 cm. Write yes or no.
flow.parent: If the magnet is weak, a coin may lift and then drop. Count a lift of 5 centimetres as yes. On a ten-rupee coin, also touch the edge of the magnet to the ring and to the centre.
flow.context: This step of the Coin Year Test is the test itself. Here you try the magnet on every coin.

flow.do: 1. For each value, count the 'yes' coins and the 'no' coins. 2. Do the same for each colour. 3. Put the coins of each value in a line by year, oldest first. 4. Look for a year where the answer changes.
flow.say: Now we check each clue. Does every coin of one value give the same answer? Does every coin of one colour? Does the year matter?
flow.kid: Count yes and no for each value. Count them for each colour. Line the coins up by year.

ask.q: Did any clue work for every single coin?
good: Golden coins were never lifted.
Silver coins mostly were, but not the centre of the ten.
Value worked for my coins, or it failed for an old coin.

flow.parent: Results depend on your coins. Most homes find that all ones and twos are lifted, and no golden fives or tens. An old coin may break the pattern. If none does, say so honestly.
flow.context: This step of the Coin Year Test is for finding patterns. Here you count the results by value, colour and year.

flow.do: 1. Look for a coin that breaks a pattern. 2. Good places to look: a two-rupee coin with eleven sides, a thick old five-rupee coin, a silver-coloured five. 3. Test any you find. 4. Write its year beside the result.
flow.say: A coin that breaks the pattern tells us the most. Is there one coin of a value that answers differently from the rest?
flow.kid: Hunt for a coin that breaks your pattern. Test it. Write its year.
flow.parent: Old two-rupee coins with eleven sides are not attracted. Nor are thick old five-rupee coins. A thin silver-coloured five from the late 2000s may be attracted. If you have none, the next step tells your child about them.
flow.context: This step of the Coin Year Test is a hunt for a coin that breaks the pattern.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for the three sentences. 2. Ask why two coins of one value could answer differently. 3. Only then read 'Indian coins are made of four different alloys' together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. What could make two coins of one value different?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The magnet lifts a one-rupee coin and not a ten-rupee coin. What does that tell you about the two coins?
good: They are made of different metals.
The one-rupee coin has iron in it, in a form a magnet attracts.

ask.q: Why might a mint change the metal of a coin and keep its value?
good: The old metal became too costly.
Steel is cheaper than copper and nickel.

flow.parent: The value is stamped on the coin by people. The magnet answers only to the alloy. Coins of one value can be different alloys in different years.

check.q: A magnet lifts one two-rupee coin and not another. What is the best explanation?
options: One of the coins is fake
The magnet got weaker
The two coins are different alloys
check.why: Two-rupee coins were cupronickel until the mid-2000s and stainless steel after that. A magnet attracts only the steel. Choosing 'fake' means trusting the stamped value more than the test.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Coin Year Test. Here you explain your results.

experiments.title: Can You Tell by Looking? Three clues against the magnet
experiments.context: In this experiment you collect 12 metal things. You write down three clues you can see or hear: colour, shine and whether people call the thing steel. Then you test each thing with a magnet, to find out whether any clue gives the answer.
experiments.question: Can you tell whether a magnet will attract a metal thing from its colour, its shine or its name?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which clue will work best: 'silver-coloured things are magnetic', 'shiny things are magnetic' or 'things called steel are magnetic'? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the thing being tested. Use the same magnet and the same face of the magnet. Fill in the three clue columns for all 12 things before you pick up the magnet. Touch the magnet to each thing and pull it away slowly. Write 'yes' for a clear hold, 'weak' for a faint cling and 'no' for nothing.

materials.item: a steel nail or screw, a safety pin and a one-rupee coin
a steel plate, a steel tumbler and a steel spoon from the kitchen
aluminium foil, or an aluminium vessel or lid
something of brass or copper: a lamp, a bell, a key, a vessel or bare wire
a golden five-rupee coin and a ten-rupee coin
an iron tawa or kadai, or the metal cap of a glass bottle
the same magnet as in the Coin Year Test
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up lifts down heavy vessels and the tawa. Test a tawa only when it is cold.

schedule.what: Collect 12 metal things. Write three clues for each, test each with a magnet, and count how often each clue was right.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all 12 things. Under it, write each clue as a rule and count the things that fit it and the things that break it. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

flow.do: 1. Read the three rules aloud. 2. Ask which one your child trusts most, and why. 3. Write the guess down.

flow.kid: Touch the magnet to each thing. Pull away slowly. Write yes, weak or no.
