flow.context: This step of Can You Tell by Looking? is the magnet test. Here you test all 12 things.

flow.do: 1. Take the rule 'silver-coloured things are magnetic'. 2. Count the things that fit it. 3. Count the things that break it, both ways. 4. Do the same for the other two rules.
flow.say: A thing breaks the rule if it is silver-coloured and not attracted. It also breaks the rule if it is attracted and not silver-coloured.
flow.kid: Take one rule. Count the things that fit it. Count the things that break it. Do all three rules.

ask.q: How many things does it take to show that a rule is wrong?
good: One is enough.
The foil alone breaks the silver rule.

flow.parent: Count 'weak' as not attracted for this step. Expect every rule to be broken at least once. Aluminium foil breaks the colour rule. A brass lamp breaks the shine rule. The steel plate breaks the name rule.
flow.context: This step of Can You Tell by Looking? checks each rule. Here you count what fits and what breaks it.

flow.do: 1. Put the one-rupee coin beside the steel plate. 2. Ask what is the same about them, and what the magnet found. 3. Ask for the three sentences. 4. Only then read 'Why a magnet attracts coin steel and not kitchen steel' together.
flow.say: Look at the one-rupee coin and the steel plate. Both are silver-coloured, both are shiny, and both are called steel. Both are mostly iron. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Put the coin beside the plate. What is the same? What did the magnet find? Say why you think so.

ask.q: The coin and the plate are both mostly iron. What could be different inside them?
good: Other metals are mixed in.
The atoms might be arranged differently.

flow.parent: Let your child offer ideas before you read the explanation. Any idea about what is mixed in, or how the inside is arranged, is a good start.

check.q: A one-rupee coin and a steel plate are both mostly iron. A magnet attracts only the coin. Why?
options: The plate has no iron in it
Their iron atoms are packed differently
The coin is heavier for its size
check.why: In coin steel the iron atoms are packed as in plain iron, and their tiny magnets line up. In kitchen steel, nickel or manganese changes the packing, and they do not line up. Choosing 'no iron' follows the rule that iron always means magnetic, which the plate breaks.

flow.context: This is the last step of Can You Tell by Looking? Here you compare a coin and a steel plate.

experiments.title: The Bent Spoon: can bending change what a magnet does?
experiments.context: In this experiment you bend a steel spoon handle back and forth, and test one spot with a magnet after every few bends. You find out whether the same steel can answer a magnet differently after it is bent.
experiments.question: Does bending a steel spoon handle change how a magnet answers the bent spot? How many bends does it take?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the bent spot answer the magnet differently from before? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Use one spoon, one spot and one magnet face every time. Touch the magnet to the spot before bending and after every 4 bends. Also test a spot 5 centimetres away that is never bent. Write 'yes', 'weak' or 'no' each time.
results_table: Magnet at the spot that is never bent

materials.item: a steel spoon that the magnet does not attract, or attracts only faintly, at its handle
a magnet that can lift a steel spoon by its handle
a cloth for the grown-up's hand
a marker pen
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the bending, with a cloth over the spoon. The bent spot gets warm and may have a sharp edge. Use an old spoon that you do not need.

schedule.what: Choose a spoon, test it, bend it 20 times in rounds of 4, and test after every round.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for every round. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. If nothing changed, write that, and say why that is also a result.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how a faint cling grows with bends
example_chart.y: Cling at the bent spot (0 = none, 2 = clear)
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your spoon may show no change at all.

setup.art: A steel spoon on a table with a marker dot on the handle where it will be bent, and a second dot 5 centimetres away.
setup.caption: 1. Mark two spots on the handle. Test both with the magnet.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands, with a cloth, bending the handle of a steel spoon at the marked dot.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up bends the handle at the first dot, back and forth.

setup.art: A magnet touching the bent dot on a spoon handle, and a notebook table beside it with a row of rounds.
setup.caption: 3. After every 4 bends, test both spots again.

flow.do: 1. Test several spoons with the magnet at the handle. 2. Choose one that gives 'no' or 'weak'. 3. Mark two dots on the handle, 5 centimetres apart. 4. Test both dots and write the answers in row 0.
flow.say: We need a spoon that the magnet does not attract strongly. Test the handles and choose one. Then mark two dots.
flow.kid: Test the spoon handles. Choose one the magnet leaves. Mark two dots.
flow.parent: If every spoon in your kitchen clings strongly, they are probably a magnetic steel. Then this test cannot show a change. Write that down as your result. Ask a neighbour for a spoon stamped 18/8 or 304.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bent Spoon. Here you choose a spoon and test it before bending.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child thinks will happen to the bent dot. 2. Write the guess and the reason.
flow.say: We will bend the handle again and again at one dot. Will the magnet answer the dot differently? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Will bending change what the magnet does? Say why. Write it down.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Bending only changes the shape.
Bending squeezes the atoms, so something may change.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Both answers are reasonable. The test will show which one is right for your spoon.
flow.context: This step of the Bent Spoon is for guessing before you bend.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up bends the handle at the first dot, about 45 degrees one way, then the same the other way. That is 2 bends. 2. Do 4 bends. 3. Touch the magnet to each dot. 4. Write the answers. 5. Repeat until 20 bends.
flow.say: Bend 4 times. Test both dots. Write yes, weak or no. Do this five times, up to 20 bends.
flow.kid: A grown-up bends 4 times. Test both dots. Write the answers. Repeat.
flow.wait: Do this on one day, taking breaks if the handle gets warm
flow.parent: Count a bend each time the handle moves one way. Let the handle cool before you test, because a warm spoon can mislead you. A faint cling may show first as a small pull when you pull the magnet away.
flow.context: In this step of the Bent Spoon a grown-up bends the handle and you test after every 4 bends.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table. 2. Find the round where the bent dot first changed. 3. Compare it with the dot that was never bent. 4. Ask for the three sentences and read 'Why a magnet attracts coin steel and not kitchen steel' together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Did the bent dot and the other dot answer the same?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Did the bent dot change? Did the other dot change?

ask.q: The spoon is the same steel along its handle. What could make one spot answer differently?
good: Bending changed how the atoms are packed there.
The metal at the bend is squeezed.

flow.parent: In some steels, such as 304, hard bending changes part of the iron to the packing that a magnet attracts. So a faint cling can appear at a bend, and the rest of the spoon stays the same. If nothing changed, your spoon may be a steel that does not change, or the bending was too gentle. A spoon that already clings strongly is a different steel.

check.q: After many bends, a steel spoon clings faintly to a magnet at the bend only. What is the best explanation?
options: The bend changed how the iron atoms are packed there
Bending added iron to the spoon
Warm metal is always magnetic
check.why: No iron was added. The same atoms were pushed into a different pattern at the bend, and a different pattern lets the tiny magnets of neighbours line up. Choosing 'warm' mixes up heat with packing.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Bent Spoon. You compare the bent dot with the dot that was never bent.

activities.title: Four Coins and a Magnet
activities.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. You guess which of four Indian coins a magnet will lift, and then test them.

materials.item: a one-rupee, a two-rupee, a golden five-rupee and a ten-rupee coin
a magnet that can lift a steel spoon by its handle, or 3 paper clips in a chain
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Draw the four coins in a row. Write 'lifted' or 'not lifted' under each one, and your guess beside it.

setup.art: Four Indian coins in a row on a table: a one-rupee, a two-rupee, a golden five-rupee and a ten-rupee coin, with a pencil guess written under each.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the four coins in a row. Write a guess under each.

setup.art: A child's hand lowering a round magnet onto each coin in turn, with the one-rupee coin already clinging to it.
setup.caption: 2. Touch the magnet to each coin. Lift it 5 centimetres.

flow.do: 1. Lay the four coins in a row. 2. Ask which coins the magnet will lift. 3. Write each guess and its reason.
flow.say: Look at these four coins. All are metal. Which will the magnet lift? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which coins will the magnet lift? Write a guess under each. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: All metal coins stick to magnets.
Silver-coloured ones are steel.
Only the big ones stick.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children say all four, or none.
flow.context: This is the first step of Four Coins and a Magnet. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Touch the magnet to the first coin. 2. Lift the magnet 5 centimetres. 3. Write 'lifted' or 'not lifted'. 4. Do the same for the other three.
flow.say: Touch the magnet to each coin. Lift it slowly. Write what happens to each coin.
flow.kid: Touch the magnet to each coin. Lift it up. Write what happened.
flow.parent: Expect the one-rupee and two-rupee coins to be lifted. The golden five-rupee and the ten-rupee coin stay on the table. An old coin may differ.
flow.context: In this step of Four Coins and a Magnet you test the four coins with a magnet.

flow.do: 1. Compare the results with the guesses. 2. Ask the question below. 3. Say that the next activities find out what is different about the coins.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. All four coins are metal. What is different?
flow.kid: What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think so?

ask.q: All four coins are metal. Why did the magnet lift only two?
good: They are made of different metals.
Some coins have iron in them and some do not.

check.q: A magnet lifts a one-rupee coin and leaves a five-rupee coin. What does that show?
options: Heavier coins are harder to lift
The two coins are different metals
The magnet works only on small coins
check.why: The one-rupee coin is steel and the golden five-rupee coin is a copper alloy. Choosing 'heavier' or 'small' follows size, but a magnet answers to the metal.

flow.context: This is the last step of Four Coins and a Magnet. You compare your guesses with what happened.

activities.title: Two Nails, Then the T Test
activities.context: In this activity you find out that a steel nail is attracted by a magnet but is not a magnet. Then you use the T test to tell a magnet from a plain steel bar.

materials.item: 2 steel nails or long screws, about the same size
a bar magnet, or a strong magnet in the shape of a stick
3 small steel paper clips
paper and tape, for the grown-up to wrap the bars

activities.record: Draw the T test. Mark which bar was the magnet, and write why the bar's end held on to the other bar's middle.

setup.art: Two steel nails lying side by side on a table, not touching, with a small gap between them.
setup.caption: 1. Put two nails side by side. Nothing happens.

setup.art: Two paper-wrapped bars of the same size, one touching the other at a right angle in the shape of the letter T.
setup.caption: 2. Touch the end of one bar to the middle of the other, like the letter T.

flow.do: 1. Lay two nails side by side, 2 centimetres apart. 2. Push them slowly together. 3. Then touch one nail to the magnet and hold a paper clip to the nail.
flow.say: First, put two nails side by side. Do they pull on each other? Then put one nail on the magnet. Can that nail lift a paper clip?
flow.kid: Push two nails together. Do they pull? Touch a nail to the magnet. Try a clip.

ask.q: The nail lifted a clip while it touched the magnet. What happens when the magnet is taken away?
good: The clip falls off.
The nail stops being a magnet, or nearly stops.

flow.parent: Two nails give nothing. A nail touching a strong magnet lifts a clip or two. Taking the magnet away drops most of them. Plain steel keeps very little.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Nails, Then the T Test. You compare a nail alone with a nail touching a magnet.

flow.do: 1. Out of your child's sight, wrap the magnet in paper. 2. Wrap a nail or screw of the same size in paper. 3. Shuffle the two bars and call them bar A and bar B.
flow.say: Both bars look the same. One is a magnet and one is a plain steel bar. How could we tell without opening them?
flow.kid: Two wrapped bars look the same. One is a magnet. How could you tell?
flow.parent: Use a nail about as long as the magnet. Any ideas are welcome. If your child suggests holding a clip to each bar, try it. Both bars will lift a clip, so that test cannot tell them apart.
flow.context: In this step of Two Nails, Then the T Test a grown-up wraps a magnet and a nail so that they look the same.

flow.do: 1. Touch the end of bar A to the middle of bar B, like the letter T. Feel for a pull. 2. Now touch the end of bar B to the middle of bar A. 3. Write which pull was stronger.
flow.say: A bar magnet pulls hardest at its ends and least in its middle. So one T should pull more than the other.
flow.kid: Make a T with the two bars. Feel the pull. Swap the bars. Feel again.

ask.q: In which T did the bars hold on harder?
good: When the magnet's end touched the other bar's middle.
The bar that held on at its end is the magnet.

flow.parent: The magnet's end touching the other bar's middle holds firmly. The plain bar's end touching the magnet's middle pulls only faintly. When you have decided, unwrap the bars to check which one is the magnet.
flow.context: This step of Two Nails, Then the T Test is the T test itself. Here you find the magnet.

flow.do: 1. Unwrap both bars. 2. Check the answer. 3. Ask why the magnet's middle is weak and its end is strong.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Which bar was the magnet?
flow.kid: Unwrap the bars. Were you right? Say why the T test works.

check.q: In a T test, the end of bar A holds firmly to the middle of bar B. Which bar is the magnet?
options: Bar A
Bar B
Both bars
check.why: A magnet pulls hardest at its ends. So the end of bar A pulls on bar B's middle. Bar B's middle is weak even if B is a magnet. Choosing 'both' forgets that two plain nails do not pull each other at all.

flow.context: This is the last step of Two Nails, Then the T Test. You unwrap the bars and check.

activities.title: Same Coins, Two Patterns
activities.context: In this activity you use coins as atoms. You lay the same coins in two patterns and count the neighbours. Then you try a rule that works in one pattern and fails in the other.

materials.item: 20 coins of the same size, such as one-rupee coins
a sheet of paper, 20 centimetres by 20 centimetres, or bigger
a ruler and a pencil
a notebook

activities.record: Draw both patterns. Write how many neighbours the middle coin touched in each, and how many coins fitted inside the square.

setup.art: Sixteen coins laid in four neat rows and four columns, like squares on graph paper, with one middle coin touching four others.
setup.caption: 1. Lay coins in rows and columns. Each middle coin touches 4 others.

setup.art: Coins in rows where every second row is shifted half a coin sideways, so each middle coin touches six others.
setup.caption: 2. Shift every second row by half a coin. Each middle coin now touches 6.

flow.do: 1. Draw a square 10 centimetres by 10 centimetres on the paper. 2. Lay coins inside it in straight rows and columns. 3. Count the coins touching one middle coin. 4. Count the coins inside the square.
flow.say: Pattern A: straight rows and columns. Count the neighbours of one middle coin. Count all the coins inside the square.
flow.kid: Lay coins in straight rows. Count the neighbours of a middle coin.
flow.parent: A middle coin in straight rows touches 4 others. Coins that cross the line of the square do not count as inside.
flow.context: This is the first step of Same Coins, Two Patterns. You make the first pattern.

flow.do: 1. Pick up the coins. 2. Lay them again in rows, with every second row shifted half a coin sideways. 3. Count the neighbours of a middle coin. 4. Count the coins inside the square.
flow.say: Pattern B: shift every second row. Now count the neighbours of a middle coin. Count the coins inside the square.
flow.kid: Shift every second row by half a coin. Count the neighbours. Count the coins.

ask.q: Both patterns use the same coins. What is different?
good: Each coin touches 6 neighbours, not 4.
More coins fit in the same square.

flow.parent: A middle coin now touches 6 others, and usually one or two more coins fit in the same square. Real iron atoms are packed in three dimensions. There the two patterns have 8 and 12 neighbours.
flow.context: In this step of Same Coins, Two Patterns you make the second pattern with the same coins.

flow.do: 1. Make pattern A again with 9 coins in 3 rows of 3. 2. The rule: two touching coins must show different faces, one heads and one tails. 3. Try to follow the rule. 4. Then try it in pattern B with 3 coins that all touch one another.
flow.say: Here is a rule. Every two coins that touch must show different faces. Does the rule work in pattern A? Does it work for a triangle of three touching coins?
flow.kid: Touching coins must show different faces. Try it in rows. Try it in a triangle.

ask.q: Why can three touching coins never follow the rule?
good: Each coin must differ from both the others, but there are only two faces.
Two of the three must show the same face.

flow.parent: In rows, you can alternate faces like a chess board. In a triangle of three touching coins there are only two faces, so two coins must match. This is a model of one thing only: a pattern can make a rule easy or impossible. It is not how steel works. In steel the rule between neighbours is different, and it is hard to work out.
flow.context: In this step of Same Coins, Two Patterns you try a rule on both patterns.

flow.do: 1. Ask for the three sentences. 2. Ask what the coins stand for. 3. Only then read 'Why a magnet attracts coin steel and not kitchen steel' together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. The same coins gave two patterns. What could the coins stand for?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The coins did not change. What changed?
good: The pattern.
How many neighbours each coin touched.

check.q: Coin steel and kitchen steel hold the same iron atoms. What can make them answer a magnet differently?
options: The atoms are packed in a different pattern
The atoms are bigger in one of them
One of them holds no iron
check.why: Added metals such as nickel or manganese change how the iron atoms pack. That changes what the tiny magnets of neighbours can do. Choosing 'no iron' forgets that the plate is mostly iron.

flow.context: This is the last step of Same Coins, Two Patterns. You say what the coins stand for.

activities.title: Fool the Magnet Test
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up hides five things in balls of foil. You use a magnet to guess what is inside each ball. You find out what a yes and a no from a magnet can and cannot tell you.

materials.item: aluminium foil, 6 sheets each about 30 centimetres square
a one-rupee coin, a golden five-rupee coin, a steel safety pin and a pebble
a magnet that can lift a steel spoon by its handle
a pencil and a notebook

activities.record: Make a table of five balls. Write your guess for each ball, the magnet's answer, and what was inside.

setup.art: Five small crumpled balls of aluminium foil in a row, numbered 1 to 5 with a pencil on a paper strip beside each.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up wraps five things in foil and numbers the balls.

setup.art: A child touching a magnet to a ball of foil, with the ball clinging to it, and a notebook table beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Touch the magnet to each ball. Write yes or no.

flow.do: 1. Out of your child's sight, wrap the coin, the pin and the pebble each in one sheet of foil. 2. Wrap the golden five-rupee coin in one sheet. 3. Wrap the second one-rupee coin in four sheets, packed tight. 4. Number the five balls.
flow.say: I have hidden five things, each wrapped in foil. Ball 1 holds a one-rupee coin and ball 2 holds a golden five-rupee coin. Ball 3 holds a pin and ball 4 holds a pebble. Ball 5 holds a one-rupee coin under many layers of foil. Which balls will the magnet say yes to?
flow.kid: Five things are hidden in foil. Which will stick to the magnet? Guess.
flow.parent: You need two one-rupee coins. One goes in ball 1, wrapped in a single sheet of foil. The other goes in ball 5, wrapped in four sheets, until the ball is about as big as a walnut. Keep a note of what is in each ball.
flow.context: In this step of Fool the Magnet Test a grown-up hides things in balls of foil.

flow.do: 1. Touch the magnet to ball 1. 2. Pull it away slowly. 3. Write yes, weak or no. 4. Do the same for balls 2 to 5. 5. Write a guess for what is inside each one.
flow.say: Test each ball. Write yes, weak or no. Then guess what is inside each ball.
flow.kid: Touch the magnet to each ball. Write yes, weak or no. Guess what is inside.

ask.q: A ball says yes. Does that tell you what the ball is made of?
good: No. It only says there is something magnetic inside.
It could be a coin or a pin.

flow.parent: Balls with the one-rupee coin in one sheet and with the pin should cling. The golden five-rupee coin and the pebble should not. The thick ball may give only a weak answer, or none.
flow.context: This step of Fool the Magnet Test is the magnet test on the five foil balls.

flow.do: 1. Unwrap each ball. 2. Compare with your guess. 3. Ask the questions below. 4. Count how many guesses were right.
flow.say: Unwrap the balls. Which guesses were right? Which ball fooled the magnet? Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Unwrap the balls. Which guesses were right? Which ball fooled the magnet?

ask.q: Ball 5 held a one-rupee coin. Why might it have said no or weak?
good: The coin was too far inside.
The thick foil kept the coin too far from the magnet.

ask.q: A ball of foil clung to the magnet. Foil is not magnetic. Why did it cling?
good: A magnetic thing was hidden inside.
A steel coin or pin was inside.

check.q: A magnet says 'no' to a thing. What can you be sure of?
options: Nothing magnetic is within its reach
The thing is not made of metal
The thing holds no iron at all
check.why: A no shows only that nothing magnetic enough is near the magnet. A coin deep inside a thick ball gives a no. A steel plate that holds iron also gives a no.

flow.context: This is the last step of Fool the Magnet Test. You unwrap the balls and see which one fooled the magnet.

activities.title: Read the Stamp: 304, 202 and 430
activities.context: In this activity you look for the numbers stamped on steel vessels at home. You test each vessel with a magnet, and find out whether the stamp and the magnet agree.

materials.item: 5 or more steel vessels, spoons or tumblers, with a stamp on the base or the handle
the same magnet as in Can You Tell by Looking?
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera, to read small stamps
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Make a table: the vessel, the stamp, and the magnet's answer (yes, weak or no). Then circle every vessel where the stamp and the magnet seem to disagree.

setup.art: The underside of a steel plate with a small stamp reading SS 304, and a magnifying glass over it.
setup.caption: 1. Turn each vessel over. Find the stamp.

setup.art: A child touching a magnet to the base of a steel tumbler and writing yes, weak or no in a notebook table.
setup.caption: 2. Touch the magnet to the base, the side and the rim. Write the answer.

flow.do: 1. Collect 5 or more steel things. 2. Turn each over and find any stamp. 3. Copy the stamp, such as SS 304, 18/8, 202 or 430. 4. Mark 'no stamp' if there is none.
flow.say: Most stainless steel has a number or a stamp such as 304, 202, 430 or 18/8. Let's find the stamps in our kitchen.
flow.kid: Turn each steel thing over. Find the stamp. Copy it into a table.
flow.parent: Many vessels carry no stamp at all. Stamps on cheap vessels are not always true. A magnet cannot prove the stamp, but it can show that something is wrong. Meaning of the stamps: 304 or 18/8 holds about 18 parts chromium and 8 parts nickel in 100, and a magnet hardly attracts it. 202 holds less nickel and more manganese, and a magnet attracts it faintly or not at all. 430 holds chromium and no nickel, and a magnet attracts it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Read the Stamp. You collect the steel things and copy their stamps.

flow.do: 1. Ask which stamps your child expects the magnet to attract. 2. Write the guess for each stamp. 3. Write the reason.
flow.say: Which of these steel things will the magnet attract? Which will it leave? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which steel things will stick? Write a guess for each. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: All steel has iron in it.
Steel plates did not stick before.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. In Can You Tell by Looking?, a steel plate gave no answer and a one-rupee coin gave yes.
flow.context: This step of Read the Stamp is for guessing before you test.

flow.do: 1. Touch the magnet to the base of each vessel. 2. Test the side. 3. Test the rim. 4. Write yes, weak or no for each spot.
flow.say: Test three spots on each: the base, the side and the rim. Write yes, weak or no for each spot.
flow.kid: Touch the magnet to the base, side and rim. Write yes, weak or no.
flow.parent: Rims, bases and handles are often pressed or welded, and can answer differently from a flat side. If two spots give different answers, write both.
flow.context: This step of Read the Stamp is the magnet test on each vessel.

flow.do: 1. Line up the table. 2. Find the vessels where stamp and magnet agree. 3. Find the ones where they seem to disagree. 4. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Where do the stamp and the magnet disagree?
flow.kid: Where do the stamp and the magnet disagree? Say why you think so.

ask.q: A vessel is stamped 304 but a magnet clings strongly to it. What could that mean?
good: The stamp may be wrong.
It may be a different steel, such as 430.

check.q: A magnet sticks to a steel vessel stamped 304. What is the best conclusion?
options: The vessel is probably not the steel it says
The vessel must be better steel
The magnet is too strong to trust
check.why: 304 steel is hardly attracted, so a strong cling is a warning. It is not proof, because bending a vessel can make a faint cling. Choosing 'better steel' repeats the old idea that a strong magnet means quality.

flow.context: This is the last step of Read the Stamp. You compare the stamps with what the magnet found.

projects.title: The Coin Sorter: build a machine that sorts by metal
projects.context: In this three-day project you build a coin sorter from a shoe box, like the machine in the story The Coin That Went the Wrong Way. You test how well it sorts, and write down every mistake.

materials.item: a shoe box with a lid
a piece of stiff cardboard, 20 centimetres by 12 centimetres, for the slope
a strong round magnet, or 2 magnets taped together
2 small cups or bowls, and strong tape
20 mixed coins: at least 5 one-rupee or two-rupee coins and 5 golden five-rupee or ten-rupee coins
a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the cardboard and the box. Keep small magnets and coins away from children under three.

schedule.what: Build the slope and fix the magnet under it. Test it with 5 coins.
Run all 20 coins through twice. Write down every mistake.
Fix the biggest problem, run the coins again, and work out the percentage sorted correctly.

projects.record: Draw your machine. Write the run results in a table: the coins run, the coins sorted correctly and the mistakes. Write the percentage correct for each run, and what you changed.

setup.art: A shoe box lying on its side with a cardboard slope taped inside, a round magnet taped under the slope halfway down, and two cups at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a cardboard slope in the box. Fix the magnet under the middle of the slope.

setup.art: A coin sliding flat down the slope, stopping above the magnet, with a second coin passing over it and dropping into a cup.
setup.caption: 2. A steel coin stops above the magnet. Other coins slide past into the cup.

setup.art: A notebook table with two runs of 20 coins, a column of mistakes and a percentage written at the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Run 20 coins. Count the mistakes. Work out the percentage correct.

flow.do: Day 1. 1. A grown-up tapes the slope inside the box at about 30 degrees. 2. Tape the magnet under the slope, halfway down. 3. Put one cup at the bottom of the slope and one at its side. 4. Test it with 5 coins.
flow.say: We build a coin sorter. A coin slides down a slope. A magnet under the slope stops the coins it attracts. Which coins do you think will stop?
flow.kid: Build a slope. Tape a magnet under it. Put a cup at the bottom. Try 5 coins.
flow.parent: If the magnet is too weak, steel coins slide over it without stopping. Tape a second magnet on top of the first. If the slope is too steep, even steel coins slide past. Try a slope of 30 degrees. That is about as steep as a normal staircase.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Coin Sorter. You build the slope and fix the magnet.

flow.do: Day 2. 1. Count 20 coins. 2. Run them down one at a time. 3. A coin that stops above the magnet counts as 'steel'. 4. Write down every coin that went to the wrong cup. 5. Run all 20 again.
flow.say: Today we test the sorter. Run all 20 coins, one at a time. Write down every mistake.
flow.kid: Run 20 coins, one at a time. Write down every mistake.
flow.wait: Do this the day after you build

ask.q: Which coins made a mistake? What do they have in common?
good: An old coin of a different metal.
A coin that slid too fast.
A coin that stuck on the cardboard.

flow.parent: A one-rupee or two-rupee coin that slides past the magnet is a mistake of the machine. A five-rupee coin that sticks is rare. If a coin stops for the wrong reason, such as a rough patch on the cardboard, write that too.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Coin Sorter. You test the sorter with 20 coins and count the mistakes.

flow.do: Day 3. 1. Look at the mistakes. 2. Pick the biggest problem. 3. Change one thing, such as the slope, the magnet or the cardboard. 4. Run the 20 coins again. 5. Work out the percentage correct for each run.
flow.say: Which mistake happened most? Change one thing to fix it. Run all 20 coins again. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Change one thing. Run 20 coins again. Work out the percentage correct.
flow.wait: Do this on the third day

ask.q: Why change only one thing at a time?
good: Then you can tell which change helped.
It keeps the test fair.

flow.parent: Percentage correct is the number right, divided by 20, times 100. For 18 right it is 90 percent. Praise a change that made the sorter worse, if your child can say why.

check.q: A sorter stops 8 of 10 steel coins and lets 2 pass. What is the percentage of steel coins sorted correctly?
options: 20 percent
80 percent
8 percent
check.why: 8 out of 10 is 8 tenths, which is 80 percent. Twenty percent is the share of mistakes.

flow.context: This is the last day of the Coin Sorter. You improve the machine and compare the runs.

challenges.title: Beat the Cheat: catch a steel washer that looks like a coin
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Your Coin Sorter from the project sends every steel disc to the 'steel coin' cup. A steel washer would pass as a one-rupee coin. Here you add a second test, so that the washer is caught.
challenges.problem: A steel washer, the size of a coin, is dropped into the sorter. The magnet stops it, as it stops a one-rupee coin. Add a second test to the sorter so that real one-rupee and two-rupee coins pass, and the washer or any other steel disc is thrown out.
constraints: Real one-rupee and two-rupee coins must still pass.
Use only things from home: cardboard, tape, scissors and a ruler.
Measure the width of every coin and the washer, in millimetres, before you design.
Test with 10 real coins and the washer. Write down every mistake.
materials: the Coin Sorter from the project
a steel washer or a flat steel nut, or a flat steel disc, about the size of a coin
general: Cut a slot in the cardboard just wider than a one-rupee coin, so that wider discs cannot pass.
Cut a slot just narrower than a two-rupee coin, so that wider discs fall out.
Put a ruler gap above the slope, and let only discs of the right width roll through.
creative: Listen: drop each coin on a steel plate, and compare the sound with the sound of the washer.
Weigh: balance each disc against a pile of five other coins on a ruler seesaw, and compare.
Add a ramp so that a disc must roll through a narrow gate on its edge.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own second test. Test it with 10 real coins and the washer. Draw it, and write how many mistakes it made.

setup.art: A cardboard slot with a ruler beside it and a one-rupee coin passing through it while a larger washer is stopped at the slot.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a slot to the width of a coin. A wider washer cannot pass.

setup.art: A notebook page with a row of coin widths in millimetres and the washer's width circled in red.
setup.caption: 2. Measure every disc and write its width. Compare with the washer.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem together. 2. Measure the width of each coin and the washer in millimetres. 3. Write the widths in a row. 4. Ask the question below.
flow.say: The magnet cannot tell a steel coin from a steel washer. How else could a machine tell them apart? Which idea do you think will work best?
flow.kid: A magnet cannot tell a washer from a coin. What else could tell them apart?

ask.q: What differs between a coin and a washer that is the same steel?
good: The width.
The weight.
The hole in the middle.
The sound when dropped.

flow.parent: Real vending machines check several things at once, such as size, weight, how the coin carries electricity and how it answers a magnet. A washer has a hole, so the hole test is easy. Pick a washer without a hole or a flat steel disc if you can.
flow.context: This is the first step of Beat the Cheat. You measure the coins and the washer.

flow.do: 1. Your child chooses one second test. 2. A grown-up helps cut the slot or build the gate. 3. Fit it to the Coin Sorter.
flow.say: Choose one second test. Tell me exactly how wide the slot is, and where it goes.
flow.kid: Choose one second test. Build it onto the sorter.
flow.context: In this step of Beat the Cheat a grown-up helps you build the second test.

flow.do: 1. Run 10 real coins through the sorter. 2. Run the washer. 3. Write down every mistake. 4. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Run the 10 coins and the washer. Count the mistakes. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Run the coins and the washer. Count the mistakes.

ask.q: Could a clever cheat still fool your sorter?
good: Yes, a steel disc cut to the width of a coin.
Yes. No test is perfect.

flow.parent: A cheat who knows the width can cut a steel disc to match. That is why real machines check more than two things. Any test can be fooled, and more tests make it harder.

check.q: Why does a vending machine check the size and the metal of a coin?
options: One test alone is easier to fool
A magnet cannot lift a coin
Coins of every value have the same size
check.why: A steel washer passes the magnet test and fails the size test. A disc cut to the right size passes the size test and may fail the metal test. Two tests together catch more cheats.

flow.context: This is the last step of Beat the Cheat. You test the sorter with the washer.

challenges.title: Four Jobs, Four Metals: choose the right metal for each job
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Four jobs each need a metal that answers a magnet in a certain way. You choose the metal for each one and test the ones you have at home.
challenges.problem: Choose a metal for four jobs. (1) The case of a compass. (2) The base of a pan for an induction stove. (3) A pin to mend a broken bone, which a patient wears while a strong MRI magnet scans them. (4) A board that fridge magnets stick to. Give one reason for each choice.
constraints: Choose each metal from this list: iron or steel, stainless steel of the 304 kind, stainless steel of the 430 kind, brass, aluminium, copper and a titanium alloy.
A compass case must not pull the needle. An induction pan base must be attracted by a magnet.
A bone pin must be safe near a very strong magnet. A fridge board must hold a magnet.
Test every metal that you have at home. Use the results in your reasons.
materials: a steel spoon, a brass key or lamp, aluminium foil, copper wire and an iron nail
the magnet from the earlier experiments
general: Compass case: brass or aluminium, because a magnet does not attract them.
Induction pan base: a steel that a magnet attracts, such as the 430 kind or plain iron.
Fridge board: a steel that a magnet attracts, such as plain steel.
creative: Bone pin: a titanium alloy, which a magnet does not attract, or a 304-type stainless steel.
Make a pan with two layers: a magnetic steel base glued to an aluminium body, so it heats evenly.
Use a thin steel sheet behind a wooden board, so that magnets stick to a board that looks like wood.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent a fifth job that needs a magnetic metal, and a sixth job that needs a metal a magnet does not attract. Choose the metals and give your reasons.

setup.art: A notebook table with four jobs down the left side and the seven metals along the top, with ticks and crosses in some boxes.
setup.caption: 1. Make a table of the four jobs and the seven metals.

setup.art: A child touching a magnet to a brass key, a steel spoon and a ball of foil in a row.
setup.caption: 2. Test the metals you have at home. Write the results.

flow.do: 1. Read the four jobs. 2. Draw the table. 3. Ask which job needs a metal that a magnet attracts, and which needs one that a magnet does not attract.
flow.say: Four jobs need four different metals. For each job, does it need a metal the magnet attracts or one that it leaves alone?
flow.kid: For each job: does it need a metal the magnet attracts, or one it leaves?

ask.q: Why can a compass case not be made of steel?
good: The steel would pull the needle.
A magnetic case would turn the needle away from north.

flow.parent: The compass needle is a small magnet. Steel near it would attract it, and the needle would not point north. A very strong MRI magnet would also pull a steel pin out of a patient's bone.
flow.context: This is the first step of Four Jobs, Four Metals. You sort the four jobs into two kinds.

flow.do: 1. Test the metals you have at home with the magnet. 2. Write yes, weak or no in the table. 3. For the metals you cannot test, read the unit's cards on alloys.
flow.say: Test the metals we have. Write yes, weak or no. For the others, look at the alloy cards.
flow.kid: Test the metals you have. Write yes, weak or no.
flow.parent: Brass, aluminium and copper should all say no. A nail should say yes. A steel spoon depends on its steel. Titanium and the 430 stainless steel are probably not at home, so use the unit's facts for them.
flow.context: In this step of Four Jobs, Four Metals you test the metals you have at home.

flow.do: 1. Choose a metal for each job. 2. Write one reason for each. 3. Share your choices. 4. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Choose one metal for each job. Give a reason that uses what the magnet did. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Choose a metal for each job. Give one reason for each.

ask.q: Why is a bone pin made of a metal a magnet does not attract?
good: A strong MRI magnet could pull on it.
It must be safe in a hospital scanner.

check.q: Which metal is best for the base of a pan used on an induction stove?
options: Aluminium
A steel that a magnet attracts
Brass
check.why: An induction stove works through a magnetic steel base. Aluminium and brass are not attracted by a magnet, and the usual induction stove does not heat them well.

flow.context: This is the last step of Four Jobs, Four Metals. You choose the metals and give your reasons.

items.p: What is the difference between a magnet and a magnetic material?
opts: A magnet has its own field. A magnetic material is only attracted.
A magnetic material is stronger than a magnet.
A magnet is iron, and a magnetic material is not.
items.why: A magnet has a field of its own and can attract or repel. A magnetic material, such as a steel nail, is attracted but has no field of its own. Two nails do not pull each other.

items.p: Two steel nails lying side by side attract each other.
items.why: False. A nail is a magnetic material, not a magnet. In Two Nails, Then the T Test, the two nails did nothing until a magnet came near.

items.p: Bar P's end holds firmly to bar Q's middle. Bar Q's end barely holds to P's middle. Which is the magnet?
items.why: A bar magnet pulls hardest at its ends and least in its middle. So the bar whose end holds is the magnet.

items.p: Match each metal to what an ordinary magnet does to it.
items.why: Only iron, nickel and cobalt are strongly magnetic at room temperature. Most other metals are not attracted.

items.p: Sort each thing by what a magnet does to it.
items.why: Nails, one-rupee coins and tawas hold iron in a form a magnet attracts. Brass, foil and the five-rupee coin are copper or aluminium alloys.

items.p: Brass is an alloy of copper and ____.
items.why: Brass is copper with zinc. Neither metal is magnetic, and nor is brass.

items.p: Which Indian coin made today does an ordinary magnet attract?
items.why: The one-rupee coin is stainless steel. The golden five-rupee coin is nickel-brass, and the ten-rupee coin is two copper alloys.

items.p: Three of these are not attracted by a magnet. Which one is attracted?
items.why: The one-rupee coin is steel. The five-rupee coin, the ten-rupee coin and the brass bell are copper alloys.

items.p: A bowl holds 3 one-rupee, 2 two-rupee, 2 five-rupee and 1 ten-rupee coin. How many does a magnet lift?
items.why: The 3 one-rupee coins and the 2 two-rupee coins are steel. The other 3 coins are copper alloys.

items.p: Every metal thing with iron inside it is attracted by a magnet.
items.why: False. A steel plate is mostly iron and a magnet does not attract it. How the iron atoms are packed matters.

items.p: Which three pure metals are strongly magnetic at room temperature?
items.why: Only iron, nickel and cobalt are strongly attracted. Gadolinium joins them only below about 20 degrees Celsius.

items.p: Steel is an alloy of iron and a little ____.
items.why: The carbon makes steel harder than plain iron.

items.p: Put the steps of a fair test of metals in order.
items: Test one thing with the same magnet
a: Test one thing with the same magnet
items.why: The prediction comes first, so you cannot change it later. The result is written at once, and the conclusion comes last.

items.p: Three people talk about how to tell steel from other metals.

views.says: Steel is silver-coloured, so I can tell it by looking.
I test every heap with a magnet. Looks fool me.
A magnet helps, but it does not tell the whole recipe.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use one result from Can You Tell by Looking? Say what another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses a result, such as the aluminium foil that is silver-coloured but not attracted. It chooses a view and gives a fair point from another.
items.why: All three have a point. Looks are not reliable, a magnet is a good quick test, and a magnet answers only one small question.

items.p: Draw the T test with two bars. Mark which bar is the magnet and where the strong pull is.
items.a: One bar standing with its end touching the middle of a second bar, in the shape of a T. The standing bar is labelled magnet, with an arrow at the touching end.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the magnet's end touching the other bar's middle. The pull is at the touching end.
items.art: A blank page with a ruler line along the bottom, for drawing two bars.

items.p: In Four Coins and a Magnet, a magnet lifted two coins and left two. Explain why, using the word alloy.
items.a: Each coin is an alloy, a mixture of metals. The one-rupee and two-rupee coins are steel, which a magnet attracts. The five-rupee and ten-rupee coins are copper alloys, which it does not.
items.why: A strong answer says the coins are made of different alloys. It does not say they are heavier or lighter.

worksheets.title: Why the same iron answers differently

items.p: Kitchen steel holds extra nickel or manganese. What do these extra metals change about the iron atoms?
items.why: The extra metals make the iron atoms pack in a different pattern. In that pattern, the tiny magnets of neighbours do not line up.

items.p: Each iron atom is a tiny magnet.
items.why: True. A few of its electrons are unpaired, so the whole atom has a small magnetic field. One atom's field is far too weak to notice.

items.p: One iron atom is hardly attracted by a magnet, but a nail is attracted strongly. Why?
opts: The tiny magnets of billions of atoms line up and add together
A nail is heavier than an atom
The nail has more electrons than one atom has
A nail has been rubbed on a magnet
items.why: One atom's field is very weak. In a nail, billions of tiny magnets point the same way and their fields add up.

items.p: Match each alloy to the metals it is made of.
pairs: Copper, zinc and a little nickel
items.why: Every alloy is a recipe of metals, and each recipe answers a magnet in its own way.

items.p: Iron stops being attracted by a magnet when it is hotter than about ____ degrees Celsius.
items.why: Above 770 degrees Celsius the atoms shake too hard to stay lined up. Pierre Curie measured this in 1895.

items.p: Cupronickel holds nickel, which is magnetic, so a magnet attracts cupronickel.
items.why: False. The nickel atoms sit among copper atoms, and their tiny magnets do not line up. The alloy is not attracted.

items.p: A made-up coin steel weighs 60 grams and is one sixth chromium. How many grams of chromium does it hold?
items.why: One sixth of 60 is 10. So the coin holds 10 grams of chromium.

items.p: Do the tiny magnets of neighbouring atoms line up in each of these?
items: the silver centre of a ten-rupee coin
items.why: Coin steel and nails keep the packing of plain iron. Kitchen steel has a different packing. Red-hot iron shakes too much. In cupronickel the nickel is spread among copper.

items.p: Three of these alloys are attracted by a magnet. Which one is not?
items.why: Nichrome is mostly nickel, yet the chromium stops the nickel atoms lining up. The other three are magnetic.

items.p: In 1903 Friedrich Heusler mixed copper, manganese and aluminium. What surprised scientists?
opts: A magnet attracted the alloy, though none of its metals is magnetic
The alloy was lighter than water
The alloy melted in the cold
The alloy contained a lot of iron
items.why: Before then, every magnetic alloy known held iron, nickel or cobalt. Heusler's alloy broke that rule.

items.p: Why is a compass case made of brass and not of steel?
opts: Steel would pull the needle away from north
items.why: The needle is a small magnet. A magnetic case would attract it. Brass is not attracted.

items.p: Graphite and diamond are both only carbon, so a strong magnet pushes them equally.
items.why: False. Graphite is pushed away far more than diamond. The pattern of the same atoms sets the answer.

items.p: Put these in order, from the atom to the pull you feel.
items: The fields of billions of atoms add up
Each iron atom is a tiny magnet
a: Each iron atom is a tiny magnet
The fields of billions of atoms add up
items.why: Each step needs the one before it. If the neighbours do not line up, the fields cancel and the magnet finds almost nothing to hold.

items.p: Explain with atoms why red-hot iron stops being attracted, and is attracted again when it cools.
items.a: Each iron atom is still a tiny magnet. When iron is hotter than 770 degrees Celsius, the atoms shake too hard for the tiny magnets to stay lined up. Their fields cancel. When it cools, they line up again.
items.why: A strong answer says the atoms stay the same and only the lining up changes. It says that being magnetic belongs to the crowd of atoms.

items.p: Why might a mint change the alloy of a coin and keep its value?
items.a: A metal can become too costly. Steel costs less than copper and nickel. The value is a decision stamped on the coin, and it does not depend on the metal.
items.why: A strong answer separates the stamped value from the metal. It names a reason such as cost.

items.p: Three people talk about a steel vessel that a magnet clings to.

views.says: My vessels do not stick to a magnet, so they are the best steel.
A cling shows how the atoms are packed. It does not show how well the steel resists rust.

views.who: A cook with an induction stove
views.says: I need a vessel that a magnet clings to, or my stove will not heat it.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use a result from Read the Stamp. Say what one other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the stamps, such as 304 giving no cling and 430 giving a cling. It sees that no cling is not the same as good, and that induction needs a cling.
items.why: The seller treats a no as proof of quality. The scientist and the cook each name a true reason, for different jobs.

items.p: Draw two zoom circles of atoms with arrows. In one the arrows line up. In the other they do not.
items.a: Two circles, each with a grid of small balls. In the first all arrows point the same way, labelled coin steel. In the second the arrows point different ways, labelled kitchen steel.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the same atoms in both circles, and a different pattern of arrows.
items.art: Two empty circles side by side on a page.

items.p: Before 1903, every magnetic alloy that anyone had tested held iron, nickel or cobalt. What did that show?
opts: That it fitted every alloy tested so far, and that is all
That no other magnetic alloy can exist
That Heusler's alloy must hold iron
items.why: A rule that fits many things can still be wrong. One new thing, Heusler's alloy, broke it.

items.p: In a made-up test, 6 of 6 one-rupee coins were lifted. A two-rupee coin from 1998 was not. What does it show?
opts: The value of a coin does not tell you the answer
The coin was lighter than the others
items.why: Two-rupee coins from 1998 are cupronickel, and newer ones are steel. One coin of a value that answers differently is enough to break the rule 'value tells the answer'.

items.p: A magnet that does not stick to a chain proves the chain is real gold.
items.why: False. Brass and copper do not stick either. A 'no' rules out steel and nothing more.

items.p: In the Bent Spoon, why test a spot 5 centimetres away that is never bent?
opts: To compare, so that bending is the only change
To use up the spoon evenly
Because the magnet is weak at the bent spot
To check that the spoon is clean
items.why: Without the unbent spot, a cling could come from the spoon or the magnet. The comparison shows that bending caused the change.

items.p: A coin sorter was run with 20 coins and sorted 17 correctly. What percentage was correct?
items.why: 17 out of 20 is 17 times 5 out of 100, which is 85 percent.

items.p: You compare how two kinds of steel answer a magnet. What must stay the same?
opts: The magnet, its face and how you bring it near
The size of the steel pieces only
Nothing, since the steels are different
items.why: A fair test changes one thing, here the steel. The magnet and the way you use it stay the same.

items.p: In a fair test you change ____ thing and keep everything else the same.
items.why: If you change two things, you cannot tell which one caused the result.

items.p: Can a magnet test alone settle each question?
items: Is this spoon attracted by the magnet?
Does this foil ball hide something magnetic?
Is this vessel good for health?
items.why: A magnet test answers only whether something magnetic is within reach. A fake coin of the right steel would pass.

items.p: Put these in order, from a rule to a better rule.
items: Find a thing that breaks the rule
a: Find a thing that breaks the rule
items.why: A rule is only a guess until it is tested. One thing that breaks it is enough to change it.

items.p: Three of these keep a test fair. Which one does not?
opts: Use the same magnet on every coin
Hold it the same way each time
Use a stronger magnet on a coin you expect to fail
items.why: Changing the magnet for one coin means the coin is not the only thing that changed.

items.p: One thing that fits a rule proves the rule is true.
items.why: False. Many things that fit make a rule more likely, but only one thing that breaks it is needed to end it.

items.p: Why are people asked to take off hairpins and keys before an MRI scan?
opts: The scanner's very strong magnet pulls on steel
Steel gives wrong pictures of the bones
Hairpins are made of iron only
items.why: A common MRI magnet is about 30,000 times as strong as the Earth's field. A loose steel thing would fly towards it.

items.p: A friend says: my magnet sticks to this steel vessel, so it must be poor steel. What would you ask or test?
items.a: I would ask which steel it is, and test other vessels with the same magnet. A cling shows how the atoms are packed. It does not show how well steel resists rust. Some good steels, used for induction pans, cling.
items.why: A strong answer separates 'clings' from 'poor quality', and suggests a comparison.

items.p: Design a fair test of three steel vessels. Say what you change, what stays the same and what you record.
items.a: Change the vessel. Keep the same magnet, the same face of it, and the same spots: base, side and rim. Write a prediction first. Record yes, weak or no for each spot in a table. Write a conclusion.
items.why: A strong answer names one changed thing, the things kept the same, and a table.

items.p: Three people talk about checking coins with a magnet.

views.says: The magnet is one of several checks. We also measure size and weight.
A magnet alone is enough to catch every fake coin.
Some old real coins fail the magnet test, and they are still real.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use what you know about old two-rupee coins. Say what another view has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the eleven-sided two-rupee coin, which is real and not attracted. It rejects the shopkeeper because a steel fake would pass. It says the maker's several checks are sensible.
items.why: The shopkeeper's view fails both ways: a real coin can fail and a fake can pass. A magnet is one clue.

items.p: Draw the results table for a fair test of five metal things. Add columns for the thing, prediction and result.
items.a: A table with three columns headed thing, prediction and result, and five rows with one metal thing named in each row.
items.why: A strong table has a prediction column filled in before the result column.
items.art: A blank notebook page with a ruler beside it.

items.p: Which of these can nobody yet calculate exactly from the atoms alone?
opts: The temperature where iron stops being magnetic
The number of coins in a bowl
The mass of a steel nail
items.why: Large groups of atoms behave in ways that are very hard to work out from one atom. Iron's exact temperature is one of them.

quiz.p: Which of these is a magnet, and not only a magnetic material?
quiz.why: A fridge magnet has a field of its own. A nail, a tawa and a spoon are attracted, and have no field of their own.

quiz.p: Which of these metals is strongly attracted by a magnet?
quiz.why: Iron, nickel and cobalt are strongly magnetic. Copper, aluminium and gold are not attracted.

quiz.p: A new two-rupee coin is attracted by a magnet. What is it made of?
quiz.why: Two-rupee coins made since about 2007 are a stainless steel that a magnet attracts. Eleven-sided coins from the 1990s are cupronickel.

quiz.p: Why do you write your prediction before you test?
opts: So that you cannot change it afterwards
So the test takes less time
So that the answer is always right
quiz.why: A prediction written afterwards could be changed to fit. Written first, it shows what you really expected.

quiz.p: The rule says: shiny metals are magnetic. Which thing breaks it?
quiz.why: A brass lamp is shiny and not attracted. One thing like this is enough to show the rule is wrong.

quiz.p: A one-rupee coin and a steel plate are both mostly iron. What differs?
opts: How the iron atoms are packed
How many iron atoms there are
quiz.why: Extra nickel or manganese in the plate changes the packing. Then the tiny magnets of the atoms do not line up.

quiz.p: Why does a magnet attract a steel nail strongly?
opts: Tiny magnets of billions of atoms line up
One iron atom is very strong
The nail is a magnet already
quiz.why: Each atom is a very weak magnet. In a nail, billions of them point the same way, and their fields add up.

quiz.p: A ball of foil clings to a magnet. What do you know?
opts: The ball is full of iron
quiz.why: Foil is not attracted. So a cling shows that magnetic metal, such as steel, is hidden inside.

quiz.p: A magnet does not stick to a gold-coloured chain. What can you say?
opts: It has no steel in it, but it may still be brass
quiz.why: A no rules out steel and nothing more. Brass, copper and gold all say no.

quiz.p: What is the honest thing to say about magnetic alloys today?
opts: New magnetic alloys are still being found and explained
quiz.why: Heusler alloys are still studied. Why atoms line up in one pattern and not in another is still hard to calculate.

quiz.p: Which fact shows that a rule about magnetic alloys can be wrong?
opts: Heusler's alloy has no iron, nickel or cobalt, and is magnetic
quiz.why: Before 1903 every magnetic alloy held iron, nickel or cobalt. Heusler's alloy broke the rule.

quiz.p: In a coin sorter, why might an old coin go to the wrong cup?
opts: Its metal differs from a new coin of the same value
It is older, so it is heavier
quiz.why: The magnet answers to the metal, not the value or the year. An old cupronickel coin is not attracted, though it buys the same things.

applications: Scrap dealers pull steel out of a mixed heap with a magnet. Copper, brass and aluminium stay behind and are sorted another way.
A magnet test in a steel vessel shop tells a buyer which kind of stainless steel a vessel is. Only some vessels work on an induction stove.
Vending machines, ticket machines and bus fare boxes check how a coin answers a magnet, along with its size and weight.
A hospital MRI scanner uses a magnet at least 30,000 times as strong as the Earth's. Pins in bones are made of metals that a magnet does not attract.
A compass case is brass, so that it does not turn the needle. A steel case would.
The core of an electric motor or a transformer is a soft magnetic steel with a little silicon. It follows the field and lets go quickly.
The mint chooses a coin's alloy. Steel is cheaper than copper and nickel, and a magnet tells the two kinds apart.

open_questions.q: Why do the atoms of iron line up in one pattern and not in another?
open_questions.why_open: The full reason needs quantum physics. Even the best computers give only rough answers for a real steel, so scientists still argue about the details.

open_questions.q: Can nobody work out exactly the temperature where iron stops being magnetic?
open_questions.why_open: Many atoms act together, and each one affects its neighbours. Calculating such a crowd exactly is one of the hardest problems in physics.

open_questions.q: Can strong magnets be made from common metals instead of rare ones?
open_questions.why_open: The strongest magnets today need neodymium, which is costly to mine. Work on iron and nickel layers, like those in meteorites, is still being checked by other scientists.

open_questions.q: Are there magnetic alloys that no one has thought of?
open_questions.why_open: Heusler's alloy of 1903 surprised everyone. Many similar alloys have been made since, and no rule yet tells scientists which new mixtures will be magnetic.

open_questions.q: Why do very small pieces of a magnetic metal sometimes lose their magnetism?
open_questions.why_open: Below a certain size, the tiny magnets in a piece of metal may keep changing direction by themselves. Scientists are still studying where this happens and why.

maths.problem: In a Coin Year Test, 13 of 20 coins were lifted by the magnet. What percentage was lifted?
maths.explain: 13 out of 20 is 13 times 5 out of 100, which is 65 out of 100. So 65 percent were lifted.
maths.context: In the Coin Year Test you test every coin in the house. These numbers are made up.
maths.why_maths: A percentage lets you compare two tests that used different numbers of coins.

maths.problem: A 25 gram bangle is 22-carat gold, which holds 91.6 grams of gold in every 100 grams. How many grams of gold does the bangle hold?
maths.explain: 25 times 91.6 divided by 100 is 22.9. So the bangle holds about 22.9 grams of gold and about 2.1 grams of copper and silver.
maths.context: In Alloy Bets you meet the card for 22-carat gold, an alloy of gold with copper and silver.
maths.why_maths: An alloy is a recipe, and parts of a hundred let you work out how much of each metal is in a thing.

maths.problem: The centre of a ten-rupee coin is three parts copper and one part nickel. A made-up centre weighs 20 grams. How much copper and how much nickel does it hold?
maths.answer: 15 grams of copper and 5 grams of nickel.
maths.explain: Three parts and one part make 4 parts. 20 divided by 4 is 5 grams in each part. So the copper is 3 times 5, which is 15 grams, and the nickel is 5 grams.
maths.context: In Alloy Bets, the card for cupronickel gives its recipe as three parts copper and one part nickel.
maths.why_maths: A ratio tells you how to split a whole into the parts of a recipe.

maths.problem: A coin sorter made 6 mistakes with 20 coins on day 2, and 2 mistakes with the same 20 coins on day 3. By what fraction did the mistakes fall?
maths.explain: The mistakes fell from 6 to 2, which is 4 fewer. 4 out of 6 is two thirds. So the mistakes fell by two thirds.
maths.context: In the Coin Sorter project you run 20 coins on day 2 and again on day 3. These numbers are made up.
maths.why_maths: A fraction of the old mistakes shows how much a change helped.

maths.problem: Iron stops being attracted above 770 degrees Celsius. A kitchen is at 30 degrees. How many degrees hotter must the iron become?
maths.explain: 770 minus 30 is 740. So the iron must become 740 degrees hotter, and a little more, before the magnet lets go.
maths.context: In this unit you read that Pierre Curie showed in 1895 that iron stops being attracted above a fixed temperature.
maths.why_maths: Taking one temperature away from the other tells you how much hotter than a kitchen the iron must become before a magnet lets go.

maths.problem: A made-up coin steel weighs 6 grams and is one sixth chromium. How many grams of chromium does it hold, and how many grams of other metals?
maths.answer: 1 gram of chromium and 5 grams of other metals.
maths.explain: One sixth of 6 is 1. So there is 1 gram of chromium. The other 5 grams are mostly iron.
maths.context: In this unit you read that coin steel is iron with about one sixth chromium.
maths.why_maths: A fraction of a weight tells you how much of each metal is in a thing.

maths.problem: A bowl holds 8 one-rupee, 6 two-rupee, 3 five-rupee and 2 ten-rupee coins. What fraction of the coins can the magnet rod catch?
maths.explain: The rod catches the 8 one-rupee and 6 two-rupee coins, which is 14 coins. The bowl holds 19 coins in all. So the fraction is 14 out of 19.
maths.context: In Fish for Change you dip a magnet rod into a bowl of mixed coins.
maths.why_maths: Counting the coins that can be caught shows your chance before you dip.

how_we_found_out.context: This is the true story of an alloy that broke a rule. For centuries, every magnetic metal that anyone found held iron, nickel or cobalt.
how_we_found_out.story: By 1900 many scientists treated it as a rule: a magnetic alloy must hold iron, nickel or cobalt. Then a German mining engineer and chemist, Friedrich Heusler, melted copper, manganese and aluminium together. None of the three is attracted by a magnet. Yet the new alloy was attracted strongly. He reported this in 1903. A magnetic alloy with no iron, nickel or cobalt broke the rule that people trusted. Later work showed that the alloy was magnetic only when its atoms sat in a neat, ordered pattern. In 1934 two British scientists, Bradley and Rodgers, used X-rays to show this pattern. Today scientists have made many 'Heusler alloys'. The old rule was true for every alloy tested before 1903, and it was still wrong.
how_we_found_out.who: Friedrich Heusler in Germany, and A. J. Bradley and J. W. Rodgers in Britain
how_we_found_out.when: Heusler reported his alloy in 1903. Bradley and Rodgers studied its atoms with X-rays in 1934.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a magnetic alloy must hold iron, nickel or cobalt. Heusler's alloy showed that three non-magnetic metals, mixed in the right pattern, can make a magnetic alloy.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in a furnace room in 1903 holding a small silver-grey bar against a magnet, with three jars labelled copper, manganese and aluminium on the bench behind him.

roots.context: In this unit you laid the same coins in two patterns. You found that a rule that works in one pattern can fail in the other. Here we ask what that says about the iron in a coin, and about you.

deep_truth.truth: In Same Coins, Two Patterns, one rule worked for coins in rows and failed for coins in a triangle. In the same way, the iron atoms in a coin and in a plate are alike, yet only the coin answers a magnet. Each atom is a tiny magnet, but a coin's answer comes from how the whole crowd of atoms sits together. So that answer belongs to the group, and you cannot find it by looking at one atom.
deep_truth.habit: We think that a thing's properties are inside its smallest parts. So we say 'iron is magnetic', as if each atom carried it alone, and we expect a thing with iron to be attracted.
deep_truth.evidence: A one-rupee coin and a steel plate hold the same kind of iron atoms, and a magnet attracts only the coin. Iron hotter than 770 degrees Celsius is not attracted, and it is attracted again when it cools. The atoms never change. Only the way they sit together changes.

three.who_am_i: You are a crowd of about thirty trillion cells. No single cell of you reads this page. What you do shows only in the whole crowd.
three.what_is_life: A living body does what none of its parts does alone, as a crowd of iron atoms does what no single atom does. Life is not one thing in one place. It is how many things sit and act together.
three.what_is_this_world: Much of the world that we call by one name, such as magnetic or alive, belongs to a crowd. If you look only at the smallest piece, you can miss it.

roots.thread: A one-rupee coin and a steel plate hold iron atoms that are alike. In the coin the tiny magnets line up with their neighbours, and the magnet attracts it. In the plate the packing is different, and the magnet does not. Many teachers have said that the truth of a thing is found by looking at it as it is, and not by its name. A coin's name says one rupee. Only the test shows what the crowd inside does.

science.text: Each iron, nickel and cobalt atom is a tiny magnet. A magnet attracts a piece of metal strongly only when the tiny magnets of many neighbours line up.
Different packings of the same atoms, in coin steel and in kitchen steel, give different answers to a magnet. X-ray pictures show the two packings.
Why one packing lines up and another does not needs quantum physics. Scientists still cannot calculate it exactly for a real steel.

other_view.view: Nothing in a crowd of atoms is beyond the laws that each atom follows. The crowd's answer can in principle be worked out from the atoms, with enough computing. Saying that a coin's answer belongs to the group only says that the sum is hard to do.

practice.title: Find the crowd
practice.say: Hold a coin in your hand. Look at it for a minute. Think about the billions of billions of atoms inside it. No single atom is the coin. Now put your other hand on your chest. Feel your heart beat. No single cell of yours beats it alone. Notice the crowd.

playtest: The experiments, activities and games were reasoned through step by step, as a family in a flat would do them. They have not yet been tried at home. The Coin Year Test (core) needs coins of several values and years. Most homes find that every one-rupee and two-rupee coin is lifted and no golden five-rupee or ten-rupee coin is. An old eleven-sided two-rupee coin, or a thick old five-rupee coin, may break the pattern. If a home has none, the step says so. Can You Tell by Looking? (core) needs 12 metal things. A steel plate usually gives no answer. If every steel vessel in a home is strongly attracted, the step tells the family to borrow a plate. The magnet may need to be strong enough to lift a steel spoon by its handle. The Bent Spoon is the least certain test. It needs a steel spoon that the magnet does not attract, and some steels show no change after bending. The step says that no change is also a result. The grown-up does the bending. Two Nails, Then the T Test needs a bar magnet and a nail of about the same length. Same Coins, Two Patterns needs 20 coins of the same size. The heads-and-tails rule is a model of how a pattern can make a rule impossible, and the unit says that it is not how steel works. Fool the Magnet Test and Read the Stamp need only kitchen things and foil. The Coin Sorter needs a shoe box, cardboard and a strong magnet, and a grown-up to cut. Beat the Cheat needs a steel washer.
